## Part 103: how the games drive the GE, on a PSP and in Phobos — tools/psp-ge-profile's plugin on the owner's PSP, the same records from the core (the runner's --ge-profile); a PSP's GE takes 4 to 12 times the model's time over the same lists

On branch `cursor/psp-ge-profile-2b67`, on master `a8d5640f5` (part 101, #263). Clean room: the plugin, the recorder
and the decoder are this project's own; the references were pspsdk's headers and libraries, uOFW (the GE, display,
interrupt and memory drivers, their NIDs, and how the module loader links and starts a module), and ARK-4's README,
wiki, `systemctrl.h`, its plugin loader's and launcher's sources and its own plugins' Makefiles (how it loads plugins,
what they look like). No PPSSPP or JPCSP code was read. Nothing of the PSP's behaviour changes: with no profile the
core does what it did (the Off cost below), and save states are unchanged (no field saved).

**Why.** Phobos's GE time (part 64, "The GE's time": geTime()) is Sony's peaks, four pixels or 35/166 of a primitive a
bus clock, the least a PSP could take, because nothing measured on a PSP said more. Chains of Olympus paces its loop
by the GE (part 64, "Why the menu drew 28 million fours"): it draws its menu's scene two or three times a vblank in
Phobos, and Vulkan draws each of them (at 5x, most of a frame's GPU time). Whether a PSP draws it once, or as often,
decides both the accuracy and that work. tools/psp-ge-profile records how a game drives the GE and the display on the
owner's PSP; the core now records the same in Phobos, and one decoder prints both.

### The plugin (tools/psp-ge-profile; its README has the details)

A kernel module for ARK-4's plugin loader. It finds the firmware's GE and display functions through ARK's
`sctrlHENFindFunction` and patches their syscalls (`sctrlHENPatchSyscall`), so every call a game makes to
sceGeListEnQueue(Head), sceGeListUpdateStallAddr, sceGeListSync, sceGeDrawSync, sceGeListDeQueue, sceGeBreak,
sceGeContinue, sceGeSetCallback/UnsetCallback, sceDisplaySetFrameBuf and the vblank waits goes through a hook: six
instructions straight into the firmware's function while idle (sceDisplaySetFrameBuf's, which also notes each flip for
the notices, some tens); while capturing, a 32-byte record with the call's entry
and return times (sceKernelGetSystemTimeLow), its thread, arguments, result, the vblank count and the GE's state (the
firmware's own sceGeDrawSync(1), and the GE's next command while it draws). The GE's FINISH and SIGNAL callbacks and
the vertical blanks come from the interrupt manager's sub-interrupt monitor, registered only while capturing. Records
go to kernel memory and the file (`PHOBOS/PROF/<disc id>-<n>.bin`, a 256-byte header, the records, a thread table) is
written after the capture at the lowest priority. A dry mode only counts calls and writes a report. Captures start by
a button combination held a second, or at a time after the game starts. It shows short notices on screen and keeps a
trace of its steps (`PHOBOS/trace.txt`). `decoder/geprof.py` (Python, standard library only) prints per vblank and per
second the lists, each list's GE time (from when the GE could begin it to its FINISH, or to the sync that waited for it
when it has no callback), the GE's busy share, the CPU's time blocked in syncs and vblank waits, flips and displayed
frames.

Bringing it up on the owner's PSP took four trips: 0.1.0 wrote nothing (a thread that looked for the memory stick's
folder once, as the game booted); 0.2.0 added the notices and the trace, and still showed nothing from a line naming
Chains of Olympus's three IDs; a load test (`hello/`: modules that only append a line) and 0.2.1 (the trace written
from `module_start`) were ready when 0.2.0 loaded from a line with his copy's ID alone. ARK-4's r205 source reads
several IDs on a line; one ID a line is what worked, and what the README now says. 0.2.2 asks for the disc ID again at
the game's first flip (ARK reads it from the disc, unreadable as the game boots: 0.2.0's trace said UNKNOWN) and holds
its start notice until then (0.2.0's flickered through the boot, drawn the other way, and was over by the game's first
frame). The captures below were all 0.2.0's, with the owner's `buffer = 192`. 0.2.3 (256 KB kept free, not 512) and
0.2.4 came after them, 0.2.4 from the review: its memory defaults are that 192 KB buffer with 256 KB kept free
(0.2.3's 2 MB would have taken all but those 256 KB of the 560 to 580 KB a game leaves free), and a boot capture's
128 KB with 320 kept, from 4 s after the plugin (where the owner's whole boot capture began) for 12 s, while the game
loads its modules: the smaller buffer is what leaves the game room then, about 430 KB where that capture's 192 KB left
about 380; the boot capture's result notice stays up its full time (0.2.2 put the start notice over it at the game's
first flip); a call from an interrupt handler is filed under `interrupt` (`sceKernelIsIntrContext`: the thread ID the
firmware gives there is an error code, 0x80020064); a file is opened as a new one only and removed if its writing
fails; the trace stops at 256 KB. None of 0.2.1 to 0.2.4 has run on a PSP yet.

### What the PSP said

The owner's PSP-1000 (model 0), firmware 6.61, ARK 4.20.69 r205 (cIPL), Chains of Olympus UCAS40198 (the Asian disc,
an ISO), two dry runs of 10 seconds on its menus: all 17 hooks in place and the monitor; the game's first flip through
the hook 4.35 s after the plugin started; a hook's cost 24 ns idle, about 1.85 microseconds capturing; a 10-second
capture's records 52 KB, with some 580 KB of kernel memory free. Each window: **357 sceGeListEnQueue, 357
sceGeListSync, 357 sceDisplaySetFrameBuf, 600 vertical blanks, no vblank wait, no GE callback**: one list, one sync,
one flip a loop, 35.7 loops a second, 0.6 a vblank. The loop part 64 read from the game's code, at a quarter of
Phobos's pace (below).

### The same records from the core

`ares/psp/kernel/geprofile.cpp` and `GeProfile` (kernel.hpp): a host hands the kernel a profile
(`geProfileStart()`), and until `geProfileStop()` it records what the plugin records, in its format:
- **The calls.** The ten sceGe_user functions and seven display functions above begin with a `ProfiledCall`: with a
  profile, a record begun with the call's arguments (profile.h's: a frame buffer's format with its sync mode above it,
  callbacks as their SIGNAL and FINISH functions), its thread (the profile's table, by UID, names as the kernel has
  them) and the GE's state (sceGeDrawSync(1)'s answer, the GE's next command while it draws); finished as the function
  returns, with v0, or, if its thread waits in it, as `switchTo()` gives the thread the CPU back with the wait's result
  (`Thread::geProfileCall`). A wait whose callbacks run first (one notified before it, or as it returns at once) has
  its record put aside with the wait while they run (`Thread::geProfileCallAside`, in `runCallbacks()` and
  `backFromCallbacks()`), so the call still ends where its thread goes on from it, with what it gave, and a call one of
  those callbacks makes is recorded as its own. sceGeSetCallback's functions are read only as the function reads them,
  with a slot free for them, and only from main RAM, where a read changes nothing. Times are
  sceKernelGetSystemTimeLow's microseconds; an end is never 0, the format's mark of a call that hasn't ended (the
  plugin's guard alike).
- **The callbacks.** A FINISH's or SIGNAL's callback is recorded as the driver queues it (`geCall()`: its callback
  number, the FINISH's or SIGNAL's low 16 bits, where the list had got to past the END, a SIGNAL's own word), from when
  the call into the program starts to when it returns (`Call::profile`, `callProfile`).
- **The vertical blanks**, each at its own time, with the count.
- **The model's charges** (kind 64, Phobos's own): each piece of drawing geTime() charges the GE for, its pixels,
  primitives and cycles, when the GE is then done with all it has, and the list it runs. On a PSP that time is
  measured; here it's charged, and this says what for.
- **Off.** With no profile, each place tests the pointer (or, in `switchTo()`, a thread's record number, always 0): the
  profiled functions, the context switch, the vblank, a call into the program starting and returning, geTime() and a
  callback queued. Measured below. Not saved: a state loaded drops the record numbers it would hold. A program that
  starts itself again (sceKernelLoadExec, `loadExec()`) ends the profile, its clock and threads starting again: one
  profile is one program's.
- **The runner** (`--ge-profile FILE`, `--ge-profile-from F`): the profile from frame F to the run's end (or to where
  the program starts itself again, the summary saying at which frame), the file written as it ends (its version
  "phobos" and the runner's commit, the disc ID and title from the disc), even if the WAV can't be, and a summary line
  (`ge profile:`). `--ge-profile-from` without `--ge-profile` is an error. tools/psp-runner/README.md says how.
- **The decoder** names kind 64, sums the charges per list (by its ID, from its enqueue call to its end) and over the
  window ("Phobos's GE model: ... charges, pixels, primitives, ms; the share set by pixels"), adds them to `--lists`
  and the JSON, and counts each kind as the dry run does (`--counts`). The tables themselves are the same for both.
  A FINISH ends the list at the head of the queue, as the GE driver runs lists first in, first out: Killzone's lists
  lie within some 350 KB of each other and its FINISH can come from commands below its list's start, so the address
  the first decoder matched by (the list whose commands it ends, within 4 MB) gave its lists the wrong ends: in the
  owner's captures a fifth to a third of its scene lists ended as if by a sync, and as many of its full-screen lists
  took 0 ms. The lists the GE still had from before the capture, when it was busy at its
  start, end first; how many there were (0 to 8) is the count that puts the most FINISHes inside the lists they end,
  then the nearest, then the fewest: the owner's Killzone captures had 2, Phobos's profile 4 (two frames ahead in its
  fast timing; the model's own records confirm each list's end). Calls and FINISHes at the same microsecond are taken
  in the order they were recorded (Phobos can run a list whole inside its enqueue). A game that sets the same frame
  buffer at every call (Killzone) has each call counted as a frame, shown from the next vblank; and a call made in an
  interrupt handler is filed under `interrupt` (plugin 0.2.0's error-code thread IDs too).
- **Tests**: "ge profile" (tests/psp/ge.cpp): a program that sets callbacks, queues a list that draws a 64x32 sprite
  and finishes, waits for it, shows a frame buffer and waits for the vblank, recorded record by record (the sync from
  its call to its thread going on after the FINISH's callback, with what the wait gave; the callback as it ran; the
  model's 2048 pixels and 1536 cycles; the blank at its own time), the file in profile.h's layout byte for byte; with
  no profile the program sees the same and nothing is recorded: the machine ends as it does unprofiled, every
  register as each call left it (stored after each), its memory and the kernel's state the same, and to the cycle,
  which the same program without its vblank wait (where a difference in time would be taken up) shows too. A state
  loaded as the FINISH's callback runs leaves the calls under way then unfinished, and the rest is recorded as before;
  with every callback slot taken, nothing is read of what sceGeSetCallback is given. "ge profile: calls whose
  callbacks run in them": a callback notified before sceDisplayWaitVblankStartCB runs in its wait and itself waits for
  the blank in sceDisplayWaitVblankStart (recorded as its own call), the outer call ending as the thread goes on from
  it with 0; sceDisplayWaitVblankCB in the blank returns 1 after its callback, recorded to there. "ge profile: a
  callback notified in the wait" (the review's): a worse thread notifies it while sceDisplayWaitVblankStartCB waits;
  it runs in the wait, the call's record put aside meanwhile, and the call ends at the blank with 0. "programs started
  in another's place" (modules.cpp): a profile ends with the old program. Each of these fails without its fix, and three
  mutants of the recorder (a charge of 100 cycles at a callback's start, a bit of v1 flipped at a call's start, the
  reset of a loaded state's record numbers dropped) are caught. The decoder's tests: a capture of Chains of Olympus's
  loop with charges, the model's sums per list and over the window, the counts; Killzone's FINISH from below its list
  (five records of the owner's capture), the lists queued before the capture, a list run inside its enqueue, a game
  drawing into one frame buffer, interrupt handlers' calls.

**Off cost.** In the bench runner's build (O3, thin LTO, as Android builds it), master's sceDisplaySetFrameBuf is nine
instructions with no frame; the branch's is the same nine and ten more while no profile records: the pointer's load
and branch, the record's and the caller's zeroed, the test of the record at its end, and a stack frame for the calls
it would make. The other profiled functions, which had frames already, add five. Chains of Olympus's difficulty menu
makes some eight profiled calls a frame and a few context switches, against the 101.5 million instructions the
emulation thread runs a frame there: a hundred or so instructions, a millionth. Measured as part 100 measures, the
emulation thread's retired instructions a frame (300 frames from the scene's state, Vulkan fast with late frames,
master `a8d5640f5` and the branch built alike, taking turns, five rounds a side; `offcost/`): Chains of Olympus's
menu, master 101.625 M (the middle of 101.498 to 102.673), the branch 101.555 M (101.088 to 101.814), −0.07%; Super
Monkey Ball's story scene, master 416.008 M (415.993 to 416.486), the branch 415.874 M (415.434 to 417.938), −0.03%.
Round by round the branch's difference was −1.54 to +0.47%, its middle −0.07 and −0.06%: nothing to tell apart from
the rounds' own spread.

### Phobos's tables

The six scenes the owner is capturing, from their states (`~/phobos-work/scratch/cpu-round3/scenes`, ahr-legal
`psp-hires/scenes`), the branch's runner, the software renderer, 900 frames with the profile from frame 301 (10 s;
ahr-legal, from frame 240 of a boot, 360 frames from its first, the copyright screen its first 2.7 s), each table
`geprof.py` (`--counts --lists`). A loop is what the game does for each frame it draws; the frames, its flips
(Killzone sets one frame buffer each time, applied at the next vblank: its calls, of which it shows one each vblank,
59.9 a second); the CPU's part, a loop's time not blocked in a sync, for the games that sync:

| Scene (clocks) | A loop | Lists a second | Frames a second (a vblank) | GE busy (model) | CPU blocked in syncs | Charged a list: ms, pixels, primitives | CPU's part |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| coo-diff (333/166) | enqueue, sceGeListSync, flip | 159.5 | 159.5 (2.66) | 100% | 838 ms a second | 6.27, 4.16 M, 8,644 | 1.02 ms |
| gos-menu (333/166) | enqueue, sceGeListSync, flip | 247.1 | 247.1 (4.12) | 100% | 707 ms | 4.05, 2.69 M, 26,297 | 1.19 ms |
| smba-story (222/111) | enqueue, stall update, FINISH, sceGeDrawSync, flip | 434.7 | 434.7 (7.25) | 86% | 88 ms | 1.97, 0.87 M, 15,100 | 2.10 ms |
| kz-gp (222/111) | two lists, each a SIGNAL and a FINISH; the frame buffer set | 517.0 | 258.3 (4.31) | 100% | none | 1.93 (its two lists 3.57 and 0.29), 0.86 M, 8,262 | |
| a2-gp (222/111) | enqueue, two stall updates, SIGNAL, FINISH, sceGeDrawSync, flip | 252.6 | 252.6 (4.21) | 92% | 92 ms | 3.55, 1.58 M, 22,603 | 3.60 ms |
| ahr-legal (222/111), its copyright screen | two lists, each a FINISH; flip | 1,701 | 851 (14.2) | 100% | none | 0.59, 0.26 M, 11 | |

None of them waits for the vblank (Activision Hits only in its logo's movie, after the copyright screen): each draws as
fast as Phobos's GE lets it, the GE busy nearly all the time, and shows one of its 2.7 to 14 frames a vblank. Every
charge in all six is set by its pixels (four a bus clock), none by its primitives.

### The comparison: the dry runs, then the owner's captures

**The dry runs** against Phobos's coo-diff, 10 seconds each: the same loop, one enqueue, one sync and one flip each
time round and nothing else of these (no stall updates, no callbacks, no vblank waits; Phobos's records show the order
part 64 read from the code), 35.7 times a second on the PSP (0.60 a vblank), 159.5 in Phobos (2.66): 4.47 times as
often. In Phobos the loop's CPU part, its time not blocked in the sync, is 1.02 ms, the rest the GE's (busy 100%, the
CPU in sceGeListSync 838 ms a second); so a PSP's 28 ms a loop had to be its GE's (or a CPU 25 times slower), some 4.5
times the model's 6.27 ms over the same list (4.16 M pixels): about 0.9 pixels a bus clock, not four. Part 64's "Left"
guessed it; the psp-hires agent's estimate (a pixel a clock, 0.65 scenes a vblank) came close.

**The owner's captures** (capture mode, plugin 0.2.0, `~/phobos-work/scratch/psp-ge-profile/captures`): Chains of
Olympus's difficulty menu (UCUS98653-5: coo-diff itself); Ghost of Sparta's main menu (UCUS98737-1) and two later,
busier scenes (-2, -3); Super Monkey Ball's Story Mode (ULES00364-1, a system dialog at its end); Killzone's gameplay
(UCUS98646-1, -2); Activision Hits' whole copyright screen from the boot (ULUS10186-boot2), a first boot capture cut
short and the 3D main menu; and, later that day, Army of Two's gameplay (ULUS10472-1, -2, two minutes into the game:
other moments of it than Phobos's a2-gp state). Each is set beside Phobos's profile of its scene over the PSP's
window of whole seconds where the scene is: Super Monkey Ball's first 7 s, before the dialog's vblank waits; the
copyright screen, seconds 3 to 7 of the boot capture, against Phobos's first 2 s. A list's GE time is the median, from
when the GE could begin it to its end (Killzone's two kinds of list apart); on the PSP measured, in Phobos what the
model charged. The CPU's part, a loop's time not blocked in a sync or a vblank wait (for Killzone and the copyright
screen, which never sync, a loop's whole time):

| Scene | PSP: lists, frames a second (a vblank) | Phobos | A list's GE time: PSP, Phobos (times) | CPU's part: PSP, Phobos |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| coo-diff | 36.2, 36.2 (0.60) | 159.5, 159.4 (2.66) | 27.60 ms, 6.24 ms (4.4) | 7.12 ms, 1.02 ms |
| gos-menu | 33.6, 33.6 (0.56) | 247.0, 246.9 (4.12) | 29.62, 4.05 (7.3) | 9.82, 1.19 |
| Ghost of Sparta's two later scenes (no state in Phobos) | 29.5, 30.0 (0.49, 0.50) | | 32.93, 31.72 | 22.2, 31.1 |
| smba-story | 39.8, 40.0 (0.67) | 434.5, 434.3 (7.25) | 23.64, 1.98 (11.9) | 18.75, 2.10 |
| kz-gp (frames: frame buffer calls) | 64.4, 32.2 (0.54) | 516.9, 258.3 (4.31) | its scene list 24.3 (27.3 in capture 2), 3.57 (6.8, 7.6); its full-screen list 1.72, 0.29 (5.9) | 15.5, 1.93 |
| a2-gp (the captures other moments of its gameplay) | 28.9, 28.9 (0.48); capture 2 24.4, 24.5 (0.41) | 252.5, 252.3 (4.21) | 31.85 (32.65 in capture 2), 3.49 (9.1, 9.3) | 25.8 (27.3), 3.60 |
| ahr-legal, the copyright screen | 216.3, 108.6 (1.81) | 1698, 850 (14.2) | 4.46, 0.59 (7.6) | 4.62, 0.59 |

- **The same games.** Each scene's loop is the same on both: the same calls in the same order (Killzone's two scene
  lists taking turns and three full-screen ones; Super Monkey Ball's stall updates, FINISH and sceGeDrawSync), the
  same clocks (Activision Hits' copyright screen 222/111 on both: the boot capture's 333/166 at its start was read
  before the game's program had started and set its own). Army of Two's is the same up to its flip: on the PSP it
  sets the frame buffer twice a frame and, most frames, waits for the vblank, while its flip from the SIGNAL's
  callback isn't shown yet (30 frames a second while the GE takes up to some 33 ms a frame, 20 above); Phobos shows a
  frame buffer at once, so it never waits there (#271, the display's switch at the next vblank, makes it wait as a
  PSP does).
- **The GE.** On the PSP the GE is busy 94 to 100% of these windows (Killzone's 89 and 98%, Army of Two's 91 and 76%,
  its frames held by the vblank), and a list takes 4.4 to 12 times what the model charges for it. Every one of
  Phobos's charges is set by its pixels; the PSP's times say the
  primitives count too: a least-squares fit of a sum (each pixel and each primitive its own time, where the model
  takes the larger of the two) over three scenes (coo-diff, gos-menu, smba-story) gives
  **0.875 bus clocks a pixel and 104 a primitive**, against the model's 0.25 and 4.74 (Sony's peaks), and puts those
  three within 11% (27.25, 30.71 and 21.09 ms against 27.60, 29.62 and 23.64). Killzone's scene list it puts at 28 ms
  (the PSP's 24.3 and 27.3), its full-screen list at 1.0 ms (1.72: a blended pass); Army of Two's list at 33.6 ms (the
  PSP's 31.85 and 32.65, at other moments of the game); Activision Hits' lists at 1.4 ms
  (4.46), most likely for their whole-screen blended passes, whose pixels cost more than the 3D scenes' average (the
  depth copies the psp-hires agent counted there are the Vulkan renderer's own, not the game's block transfers).
- **The CPU.** In the four scenes that sync, the PSP's CPU part of a loop is 7 to 9 times Phobos's (7.0, 8.3, 8.9,
  and Army of Two's 7.2 and 7.6), where Phobos counts an instruction a cycle at 333 MHz. It doesn't pace these loops on
  the PSP: they wait on the GE, which takes longer (and Army of Two on the vblank). Killzone and the copyright screen
  never sync, so their figures (15.5 and 4.62 ms on the
  PSP) are a loop's whole time, not the CPU's; Killzone's GE is busy 89 and 98% of its windows, its frame the GE's
  there too.
- **What it means for Phobos.** With a GE that takes the PSP's time, these loops would run at about the PSP's rate:
  coo-diff's 27 ms list against its 1 ms of CPU, 36 loops a second; Super Monkey Ball's 23.6 ms against 2.1 ms, about
  42 (the PSP's 40). Each frame drawn and not shown is work for the host now: two to fourteen frames a vblank for Vulkan
  to draw, one shown.

### Left

- Ghost of Sparta's two later scenes have no state in Phobos, Army of Two's captures are of other moments of the game
  than its state, and Killzone's two captures differ a little between themselves (scene lists of 24.3 and 27.3 ms:

- A capture's memory: on the owner's PSP-1000 a game leaves some 560 to 580 KB of kernel memory free, and ten seconds

- geTime() is unchanged here: the captures say by how much it's short, not yet how a PSP's GE spends its time. The

- The CPU's 7 to 9 times in the scenes that sync: Phobos's instruction a cycle against a PSP's CPU in these loops. It
  paces none of these scenes; a model of the CPU's time is a separate question (the captures give its part of each

- The decoder counts frames by flips; a game that sets the same buffer at every call (Killzone) has each call counted

- The GE sync spin (part 105) works out a polled sceGeDrawSync or sceGeListSync without the call being made, so the

## Part 104: Activision Hits Remixed's clocks — what a PSP's power service grants a game, the bus asked for alone, and the owner's captures' 333/166, read before the game ran

On branch `cursor/psp-power-clock-2b67` (draft PR #267), on master `a8d5640f5` (part 101, #263), masters `5442acb8b`
(part 102, #265; #264, no part), `03eca2a69` (#274, no part) and `a014706e9` (part 103, #266) merged in. The question
(part 103): the owner's captures of Activision Hits Remixed's boot read 333/166 MHz, Phobos's state 222/111, which
matters once the GE takes a PSP's time (its time goes with the bus's clock). Was `scePowerSetBusClockFrequency`'s
refusal of anything over 111 the cause? Sources: uOFW's reading of the power service (its `power` branch, pull request
#82: `clockFrequency.c`, `power.c`), its reading of Init and the module manager; ARK-4's README, settings and clock
code (systemctrl's `cpuclock.c`, `syspatch.c`, `plugin.c` and `loadercore.c`, the PSP layer's `syspatch.c`, stargate's
`gamefix.c`: r205's, which the owner runs, and master's `7c03c37` the same). No PPSSPP or JPCSP. Save states are
unchanged (layout 32).

### What the game asks for, and what a PSP grants

- **The game** (the runner from boot with a scratch build noting each power call, 1200 frames): as it starts, its
  thread asks for a CPU of 333 (`scePowerSetCpuClockFrequency`) and a bus of 166 (`scePowerSetBusClockFrequency`),
  then prints what it reads back. It asks for nothing else in the 1200 frames: the copyright screen, the menu's
  loading, the startup movie.
- **The power service**, as uOFW reads it: the CPU no faster than the PLL; the bus asked for alone no faster than half
  the PLL, then set to half the PLL whatever a game asked; `scePowerSetClockFrequency` checks a PLL of 19 to 333, a
  CPU of 1 to 333 and a bus of 1 to 167, the CPU no faster than the PLL and the bus no faster than half of it. As the
  system reboots into a game the service sets every clock to its most, 333/333/166 (`_scePowerModuleRebootPhase()`),
  and so they stay while Init loads the boot modules and then the game's program; with the program loaded, before it
  starts it, Init calls its boot callbacks of levels 0 to 3 (uOFW's `init.c`, `sub_05F0()`), the power service's
  among them (level 2), which sets the startup clocks for games, 222/222/111 (`_scePowerInitCallback()`). So the
  game's first instruction runs at a PLL of 222, both of its requests are refused, as Phobos refused them, and it runs
  at 222/111.
- **The owner's PSP did the same**: the captures' 333/166 were read before the game ran. The plugin counts from its
  own `module_start`, which ARK runs as Init starts `sceMediaSync` (systemctrl's `loadercore.c`), before the game's
  program is loaded. Each boot capture read 333/166 as it began, boot1's 0.3 s after that and boot2's 4.0 s after,
  and the game's thread made its first GE call 4.0 s (ULUS10186-boot1) and 4.23 s (-boot2) after it; in Phobos that
  call (the same list, sync and callbacks) comes 3.6 ms after the program starts, with no file read before it, the
  clock requests just before it. So the program started about 4.0 s in on boot1 and 4.22 s on boot2, each after its
  own capture's reading: the 333/166 were the reboot's clocks, Init still loading the 7.6 MB program. boot1's capture,
  ended by its full buffer 9.6 s in, in the copyright screen, read 222/111 there, and the screen's lists took the same
  time from its first frame (6.3 s) to that end, and in boot2 to the screen's end: all of it at 222/111. In the menu
  (31 s) 222/111 too. With ARK's clock settings at Auto, as the owner had them, ARK neither sets the clocks nor
  touches the setters: `overclock`, `powersave` and `defaultclock` each set a level (1 to 3) that, once the system has
  booted, `SetSpeed()` applies, setting the clocks with `scePowerSetClockFrequency` and turning the game's setters
  (`scePowerSetClockFrequency` under each of its five NIDs, `scePowerSetCpuClockFrequency`,
  `scePowerSetBusClockFrequency`) into functions that return 0; with none set, the level is 0 and neither happens. On
  a PSP, ARK patches the power service only for the backlight's maximum, and its game fixes that drop the CPU setter
  are other games' (WWE SmackDown's, ATV Pro's).

### What changed

- `scePowerSetBusClockFrequency` takes a bus up to half the PLL's speed, as uOFW reads it, where it refused anything
  over 111 whatever the PLL. That changes its answer both ways: at a PLL of 333, 112 to 166 are granted now, and at
  266, 112 to 133, the bus staying at half the PLL; at 190, 96 to 111, granted before, are refused.
- `scePowerSetClockFrequency` refuses a bus above half the PLL asked for (222/222/166 was taken, the PLL set to 222;
  200/200/101 is refused though the PLL would run at 222, as the service checks the request before it rounds the PLL
  up); a bus of 167 passes the range check, as the service's does, and fails this one at any PLL, and a bus over 167
  fails the range check before its double is taken.
- Activision Hits runs as before, at 222/111: what the owner's PSP gave it. Death Jr., Death Jr. II and Sonic Rivals
  make exactly its two requests as they start, refused before and now alike.

### What it means

- Part 103's comparison of the copyright screen is at the same clocks as it stands: 222/111 on the PSP and in
  Phobos, no scaling.
- The owner's captures: a capture that starts before the game runs reads the reboot's 333/166 at its start. With
  ARK's clock settings at Auto games keep their own clocks; Overclock, Power Save or Balanced would set every game's
  and make its own setters do nothing. The captures so far are all at the games' own clocks (Chains of Olympus and
  Ghost of Sparta set 333/166 themselves, Phobos's states have them too; Army of Two sets 222/222/111 itself, 85
  vblanks after its boot; Killzone, Super Monkey Ball and Activision Hits run at 222/111).

### Tests

"power clocks" (tests/psp/power.cpp): a bus above half the PLL refused by `scePowerSetClockFrequency`, the PLL left as
it was, the PLL asked for checked and not the speed it would run at (200/200/101 refused), and a bus over 167 refused
before its double is taken (one whose double wraps to 166); the bus asked for alone granted up to half the PLL's
speed (112 at 333, the bus staying at 166), 167 refused, 112 refused at 222 and 111 granted, 96 refused at 190 and 95
granted, 133 granted at 266 and 134 refused; and Activision Hits' start, the CPU's 333 and the bus's 166 refused at a
PLL of 222, the clocks staying 222/111. The first two fail on master, and so does the test with either of the
review's two mutants that it let through before (the bus checked against the PLL's rounded speed; no range check of
a bus over 167).

### Checks

`tests/psp/run-tests.sh` (sanitized; the address sanitizer's container-overflow check off, as part 101 ran it):
579 groups, 0 failures. CI runs tests/allegrex, tests/psp/ares and the builds.

### Scratch

In `~/phobos-work/scratch/psp-ge-profile/`: `power/` (`ahr-boot.sh`, the traced boots; `ahr-boot.log`, the last);
`ref/uofw-power` (uOFW's power branch at `f7ed03aa7`), `ref/uofw/src/kd/init/init.c`, `ref/ark4-r205/README.md` and
`contrib/SETTINGS.TXT`, `ref/ark4-src` (ARK-4's sources at `7c03c37`) and `ref/ark4-r205-clock` (r205's clock files,
the same); the boot captures `captures/ULUS10186-boot1-cut.bin`, `-boot2.bin`, `-menu.bin`; `phase3/ahrstart.sh` (the
game from boot in #269's runner, its GE profiled and its files traced). The review's library trace (every power call
the 266 games make in their first 1200 frames, replayed through master's and this branch's rules: no answer changed)
is in `~/phobos-work/scratch/review-267/trace/`. Nothing was run on the RP6.

## Part 105: the GE's looks skipped through when a game polls them — sceGeDrawSync(1) and sceGeListSync(id, 1) as part 91's spins

On branch `cursor/psp-ge-sync-spin-2b67` (draft PR #268), from master `a8d5640f5` (part 101, #263), masters
`5442acb8b` (part 102, #265; #264, no part), `03eca2a69` (#274, no part) and `dd63f4ffb` (parts 103 and 104, #266 and
#267) merged in. The task (the GE timing design's first step, which the owner approved): part 76's GE timing, a PSP's
time for each list, made the games that poll the GE slower on the host, as they asked for as long as a PSP's GE
draws: on the RP6 at 5x Resistance went from 59.9 to 40.4 frames a second and Need for Speed: Shift from 45.3 to
32.9, Shift calling `sceGeDrawSync(1)` some 7000 times a frame with about 765 cycles of its own work between calls
(part 76's count). Part 91 skips loops of calls that change nothing to just before the CPU's go ends, every register,
byte and cycle as running them would give; the GE's looks weren't among the calls it could work out. Clean room: our
code, uOFW for the driver's behaviour, nothing of PPSSPP or JPCSP. Save states are unchanged (layout 32): nothing new
is kept.

### What changed

- **The looks are calm** (kernel/ge.cpp): `sceGeDrawSync` and `sceGeListSync` in mode 1, or with a mode refused, or
  a list (one refused in any mode, 0 too), change nothing (`Kernel::calm`), so the call leaves the CPU's go as it was
  and may be a spin's turn (part 91's `spinTurn()`). A wait (mode 0 with a list there, or `sceGeDrawSync(0)`) isn't
  one.
- **Their spin handlers** (spins.cpp: `spinGeDrawSync()`, `spinGeListSync()`) give the shadow the call's answer
  without making it, through the same function the call answers with (`geDrawLook()`, `geListLook()`), so the two
  can't differ; a list refused is worked out in any mode, 0 too, but a wait isn't, so a turn calling one isn't
  skipped. Neither function reads the clock: a skip answers every turn it passes with the answer it gives then.
- **The runner's `--spin-skip on|off`** (tools/psp-runner): part 91's skip, on by default, off with `--ge-profile`
  unless given. A skipped turn makes no calls, so a profile kept few of a game's polls (in the test of the looks,
  63 of 587,523 poll records); with the skip off a profile counts every poll, as the PSP's plugin records them. The
  report says which ran, so a library check can run the skip on and off in one binary.
- **Why it's exact.** What the GE and its lists are doing changes only in a system call (an enqueue, a stall update,
  a list's FINISH taken) or between the CPU's goes (the GE given more of a frame's commands, `geBusy`). A list's
  FINISH falls due at `geDoneAt`, which `untilNextEvent()` makes the go's end, and `spinSkip()` already refuses a skip
  past it; the FINISH is taken by the first call after, as before. So every turn a skip passes over would have had
  the same answer, and the turns left run as they would.

### Tests

- **"the GE's looks polled, skipped as run"** (tests/psp/spins.cpp): a program queues a list of 16 sprites covering
  the screen (each a fill the GE takes its time over) with a finish callback, then asks how the GE is doing till it
  says done, the clock noted after each; each variant queues three lists: through `sceGeDrawSync(1)`, through
  `sceGeListSync(id, 1)`, and with the list held at its start (its stall address) till a mover thread moves that to
  its end, the looks saying 3 and then 2. On both engines, with the skip on and off, the machine's whole state is
  the same after every eighth of a frame, and thousands of turns are skipped, the stalled phase's among them (some
  81,000 before the mover's turn); with a register counting the turns (a loop that isn't one turn over and over)
  none are. The finish callbacks run once a list, the clock noted moving on.
- **"the GE's looks polled behind a list, past a SIGNAL, with interrupts held off"** (the review's experiments): a
  list queued behind another and asked after till done (queued, then drawing); a list's SIGNAL callback running
  mid-poll; and polling with interrupts held off past the list's FINISH till the vertical blank comes, then on. The
  same, both engines, each skipped by the thousand.
- **"the GE's looks polled under a GE profile"**: with a profile recording, the skip on and off leave the machine the
  same and every record but the looks' the same, and with it off every look is recorded.
- **"ge FINISH after a quiet function"** (tests/psp/ge.cpp): the looks, and a mode or a list refused (a list in mode 0
  too, and a free list's ID in mode 1), are dispatched as calm, the next thing's time where it was after each.

### Checks

`tests/psp/run-tests.sh` (sanitized; the address sanitizer's container-overflow check off, as part 101 ran it):
574 groups, 0 failures (the new group's list first put where the test machine keeps its stubs, which drew
nothing: moved to the GE tests' addresses, some 196,000 looks a list for the `sceGeDrawSync` loop and 174,000 for
`sceGeListSync`'s); with master `dd63f4ffb` merged in (parts 103 and 104), 580 groups, 0 failures, the GE profile's
groups among them; with the review's fixes, 582 groups, 0 failures. CI runs tests/allegrex, tests/psp twice
(sanitized, and built as the app is), tests/psp/ares and the builds.

### What it changes

With today's GE (Sony's peaks), a list is done long before most polling loops come round many times, so little
changes now. With the PSP's GE timing (#269, part 106; the review's runs, 3,600 frames, a fixed clock, the
library's presses):
- **Resistance** polls `sceGeListSync(id, 1)` (not `sceGeDrawSync(1)`): 592,699,906 turns skipped in the 3,600
  frames (some 285,000 a frame from frame 1,800), its state at frame 3,600 the same byte for byte as with the skip
  off; the host's time 24.8 s, against 30.2 and 32.0 s with it off.
- **Need for Speed: Shift** polls `sceGeDrawSync(1)` some 45,000 times a frame, but every turn also calls
  `sceKernelWaitSema(0x109, 1, NULL)` on a binary semaphore that's free (268,404,797 times in the 3,600 frames), which
  succeeds at once and is given back in the same turn. A wait that succeeds isn't calm, so `syscall()` sets the
  detector back each turn (kernel.cpp): no turn skipped, 57.8 s with the skip on against 59.0 s off, the run the same.

### Left

- Shift's loop: a wait that succeeds at once and its signal in the same turn, a net change of zero with no thread
  waiting, made a spin's turn. Its own pull request, after this one.

### Scratch

`~/phobos-work/scratch/psp-ge-profile/sync/` (this part's draft) and `tests.sh` (the suites as the load rules let
them run); the review's runs, mutations and experiments in `~/phobos-work/scratch/review-268/`. Nothing was run on
the RP6.

## Part 107: psp-measure round 8 — the GE's time where part 76's model misses the owner's captures, and the CPU's

On branch `cursor/psp-measure-round8-2b67` (PR #270), from master `a8d5640f5` (part 101, #263), masters `5442acb8b`
(part 102, #265; #264, no part), `03eca2a69` (#274, no part), `dd63f4ffb` (parts 103 and 104, #266 and #267) and
`230c0a731` (part 105, #268) and `fe3deab82` (parts 108 and 109, #271 and #272; #273, no part) merged in. Round 8 of
`tools/psp-measure`, for the owner's PSP: what round 6 left of the GE's time, chosen by where part 76's model (fitted to
round 6, ported behind the option "GE Timing" on #269) misses the owner's captures of games (part 103), and the CPU's
own time, which in every captured scene that syncs is 7 to 9 times Phobos's. Nothing in the core changes: the program,
its test, the test programs' copy of it, and the PSP's results (below). The owner approved the plan (the design's
section 4, the CPU block with it). The fit that follows the results went with the model it fits (#269, part 106:
`tools/psp-measure/ge-fit.py`, and `ge-terms.py` for the runner's counts in place of a `--ge-terms` option, so the core
carries no counting code); the `measured8` test needs this program and that model both, so it comes after them.

### Where the model misses, term by term

A scratch build of #269's runner totalled each of the model's terms over each captured scene's profile window (900
frames from the scene's state, profiled from frame 301; the GE timing "PSP"). A piece of drawing takes the longer of
the GE's two ends, so a term counts toward the time when its end is the longer; every scene's back end is. Shares of
the GE's time:

| Scene | Against the PSP | What the time is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chains of Olympus, difficulty menu | +11% | 32-bit pixels 35%, VRAM texels 31% (its 512x512 frame buffers read back at 2 texels a pixel), the depth test 18%, block transfers 7% |
| Ghost of Sparta, main menu | +3% | VRAM texels 46%, 32-bit pixels 18%, the depth test 11%, transfers 8% |
| Super Monkey Ball Adventure, Story Mode | −59% | 32-bit pixels 27%, the depth test 22%, small textures loaded whole 12%, primitives 10%, texels 10%; its front end 78% of its back end (15,000 primitives, 84,000 words and 3,500 CALLs a list) |
| Killzone, gameplay | +77 to +98% | VRAM texels 79%: a 512x512 VRAM buffer read as a CLUT32 texture in strips 32 texels wide, 1:1 (37 of its 49 ms a scene list); its full-screen list, a 512x512 VRAM texture over the screen in strips 120 wide into 5650, 96% |
| Activision Hits Remixed, menu | +138% | VRAM texels 67% (the same CLUT32 strips), point lights 20% |
| Activision Hits Remixed, copyright screen | −9% (222/111 on both) | a 512x256 CLUT8 texture in RAM, swizzled, drawn 512 across: 65% |

- **The VRAM texture rate** (round 6's: 1.93 clocks a byte, from a 256x256 texture drawn as one sprite) carries
  Killzone's and Activision Hits' menus. At the swizzled cache rate instead, Killzone's scene list would take about
  19 ms, under the PSP's 24 to 27 (its captures as #266's reviewed decoder reads them): the strips' rate lies between
  the two. Round 6 never read a texture from VRAM in strips, as a CLUT32 texture, or shrunk.
- **Super Monkey Ball's lists aren't paced by its CPU**: on the PSP each list is built within 0.12 ms of being queued
  (one stall update, none finding the GE waiting), and the GE takes 23.5 ms more. What the model leaves out is in the
  GE: its many small textured primitives, the state set between them, and the CALLs.
- **Activision Hits' copyright screen** is within the gate: the PSP ran it at 222/111, as Phobos does (its boot
  capture's 333/166 was read before the game's program had started and set its own), where the first comparison had
  scaled the PSP's time to 333/166 (−39%). Its big CLUT8 texture drawn 512 across is measured all the same.

### What round 8 measures

A new first line of the menu, "Round 8: the GE's time again, and the CPU's (about 1 MB)". Its timed lists are round
6's kind, built once, each queued alone and timed from just before `sceGeListEnQueue` to the finish callback, every run
kept: at 222/111 and 333/166 MHz, and `time-lists` and `time-scenes` also at 333/222/166 (the CPU's clock apart from
the bus's, if the PSP grants it) and 266/133 (a third bus clock). Each record says the clocks scePower gave back.
`manifest8.txt` lists every case.

- **`time-strips`**: textures 512 texels wide drawn texel for pixel over the target's 512x256, in strips 8, 16, 32,
  64, 128 and 256 wide and as one sprite: from VRAM as 8888, CLUT32, 5650 and CLUT8 (VRAM's first megabyte, the
  screen's text: its texels don't matter); from RAM as 8888 swizzled and not, CLUT8 512x256 swizzled and not, 5650
  swizzled and not.
- **`time-textures`**: a 512x512 VRAM texture shrunk 2:1 (nearest, bilinear, in strips) and 4:1, as CLUT32, from RAM;
  stretched; mipmaps (the level chosen or set, linear between levels); perspective; a texture walked by columns; a
  texture of its own for each sprite (CLUT8 of 1, 4 and 16 KiB, 5650 of 8 KiB, CLUT4, a palette loaded each time).
- **`time-pixels`**: from round 6's textured fill, one thing varied: the depth test passing and failing (and whether a
  failing pixel still fetches its texel: failing with round 6's slowest texture), not writing; the alpha, stencil
  and color tests passing and failing; every blend equation, the destination's alpha, into 5650; the texture
  functions, color doubling; a game's pixel (CLUT8, depth tested, blended) passing, failing and into 5650.
- **`time-setup`**: squares of 8x8 to 64x64 tiling 256x256 in 3D, textured and depth tested, as games draw; in
  perspective, as strips and fans, half or all cut by the near plane, half or all culled, as slivers, bilinear,
  without a texture or the depth test, from a texture over the cache's size.
- **`time-vertices`**: the front end alone (strips of back faces, culled): each part of a vertex in each format,
  lists, fans, 8- and 16-bit indices, the same three vertices again and again (a cache of vertices?), a grid's shared
  vertices; directional, point and spot lights, one to four, with their shine; skinning, one to eight bones, 8- to
  32-bit weights; morphing; texture coordinates through the texture matrix, from positions, environment mapping;
  fog; through mode.
- **`time-state`**: 8x8 sprites with one thing set before each, as games set state between draws: TEX_FLUSH, a texture
  changed or set again, a palette loaded, TEX_MODE (GU's, with its TEX_FLUSH), a blend or depth function, a matrix,
  TEX_SYNC, the alpha test switched, each PRIM in a CALLed list, 3D triangles with their world matrix.
- **`time-lists`**: a list's own time (0 to 64 small sprites); 1 to 8 lists queued at once; one list drawn while its
  stall address is moved on 1 to 64 times, as fast as the CPU goes and each time once the GE has reached it; 16 to
  1024 CALLs.
- **`time-signals2`**: 8 to 128 sprites 64x64, 16 to 1024 sprites 8x8, or 8 to 128 triangles (half a 64x64 square),
  then a SIGNAL that lets the GE go on, then the FINISH, the signal callback's time beside the finish's: how far
  ahead of the drawing the GE's front end gets (round 6's time-signals had the callback within 84 microseconds
  after 16 sprites over the whole target, Army of Two's 0.27 ms before its list's FINISH: part 106's
  GE::Cost::Queue, 16 for now).
- **`display-start`**: what `sceDisplayGetFrameBuf` reads as the program starts, before anything is set (asked first
  of all in `main()`), and which of five frame buffers the firmware refuses from that state: 512 wide in 8888 or
  5650, the address alone, the display off, each set at once, and one for the next vblank (pspautotests'
  display/setframebuf refused a width or format set at once that isn't the one shown; whether a game's first frame
  buffer would be decides whether Phobos may refuse them, part 108).
- **`time-transfers2`**, **`time-clears`**, **`time-overlap`**: transfers 1 to 32 pixels wide and single rows, frame
  buffers copied in VRAM; clear mode over 512x256, in one sprite and in sprites 64 wide; front-end pieces (skinned
  triangles, culled) and back-end pieces (textured squares) in turn, 1, 16 or 256 at a time, and each kind alone.
- **`time-scenes`**: lists like the captured scenes', built to what the profiles show: Killzone's scene and
  full-screen lists, Activision Hits' copyright screen and menu, Chains of Olympus's and Super Monkey Ball's, and the
  two scenes part 76 changed most: Killzone's language menu's background (a 512x512 8888 texture in RAM, not
  swizzled, in one sprite 480 wide: 62 ms a frame in part 76's model) and Super Stardust Portable's intro's glow.
- **`cpu-contention`**: the CPU reading RAM, and following a chain of pointers, with the GE idle or drawing from RAM
  or VRAM; the GE drawing while a thread reads RAM.
- **The CPU alone** (`cpu.c`): `cpu-alu` (dependent and independent additions, taken branches, loads, stores, a load
  used at once), `cpu-latency` (multiplies, multiply-adds, divides, the FPU's additions, multiplies, divides and
  square roots, its loads, stores and moves, the VFPU's additions, multiplies, dot products, sines, reciprocal square
  roots, loads and stores) and `cpu-memory` (chains of pointers over 1 KiB to 8 MiB of RAM, through RAM's uncached
  addresses, in the scratchpad and in VRAM; words read and written, cached and not; memcpy), each at all four
  settings; `cpu-syscalls` (a system call, a semaphore, a thread switch there and back, interrupts held off, the
  cache written back, the GE's calls: queueing, stall updates, its looks, the display's) at 222/111 and 333/166; and
  `cpu-clocks`, what the power service gives for 13 clock requests (333/222/166 among them, and the CPU or the bus
  asked for alone past what a stock PSP grants, part 104), with the CPU's speed timed at each. `cpu-alu`'s and
  `cpu-latency`'s loops are in assembly, so each runs what its line says; `cpu-memory`'s are C (`-O2`): a chain's step
  is a load, a branch and the count's add.

### How it runs

- About 3 minutes on the PSP (the GE's part summed from the model's rates, about 1 minute; the CPU's tests, the clock
  changes and the runs' own overhead the rest). It wrote 167 KB (140 KB of records, the 25 KB manifest, the stall note),
  where the menu line's "about 1 MB" was the estimate. The program changes the clocks part of the time and puts them
  back after each test, as round 6 did.
- A list the GE hasn't finished in 5 seconds is a stall (reset, recorded, the test goes on), as since round 4.
- newlib's heap is held to 1 MiB (`PSP_HEAP_SIZE_KB`): left to itself it takes all the memory free as the program
  starts, and `cpu-memory` asks the kernel for 8 MiB (4 if that much isn't free; the records say which). Nothing in
  the program allocates from the heap, so the other rounds draw as before.
- Round 8's helpers sit beside round 6's (`timeCases8` with settings and its own runs, `awaitFinishes` for several
  lists); round 6's code is untouched but for the finish callback counting its calls.

### The test

"psp measure" (tests/psp/measure.cpp) runs round 8 after round 7, through the menu (its lines one further down), and
checks every round 8 file: whole records, as many as the tables give, each test's settings in turn with the clocks
the core grants for each (all four), every run finished, a stall update's or the last enqueue's return before the
list's finish (time-signals2's signal callback too), the CPU's loops taking time; cpu-clocks' 13 attempts, the
first (333/333/166) granted; display-start's seven words and five attempts, the next-vblank one taken. The core's
GE times are the default timing's, so the times themselves say nothing yet; the fit compares them.

### What the PSP showed (the owner's run, 2026-10-18)

The owner ran rounds 8, 7 and 6 on his PSP-1000 (`tests/psp/measurements/ge-round8`, 19 files, kept as round 6's
are). Times below are in the GE's bus clocks (microseconds times the bus's MHz) unless they say otherwise.

- **Repeatable**: round 6 again gave all 28 pictures byte for byte as in `ge-round6`; its 906 timed cases' medians
  moved 0.15% at the median (90% within 1.3%, 99% within 7.7%; the worst, 13.9%, 18-20 microsecond transfers, a
  microsecond or two of the timer; over 1 ms the median 0.10%, the worst 6.5%); the driver's statuses read the same,
  the finish 538.0 against 537.2 ms (part 1) and 269.9 against 268.7 ms (part 2). There's no earlier PSP run of round 7
  to set its files beside (part 78's open questions stand: aa-alpha the same as the core's, aa-blend 1 pixel a level
  off, aa-slopes 117 pixels, aa-axes 259, aa-3d 1008, aa-textured 1882).
- **Wide texture reads** (`time-strips`): a texture's time per pixel jumps about 4 to 7.5 times once a sprite's row
  spans 256 distinct texels (16- and 32-bit texels; 8-bit indices between 256 and 512), from the 128-wide strips at
  222/111: VRAM 8888 and CLUT32 1.4-1.6 clocks a pixel narrow, 8.4 wide (5.4 times); VRAM 5650 1.0, then 4.1 (4.0); RAM
  swizzled 8888 1.9-2.0, then 12.4 (6.2); RAM swizzled 5650 1.25, then 6.3 (5.0); RAM unswizzled 8888 7.5, then 57
  (7.5); CLUT8 from 256 to 512 indices 3.9 to 4.1 times (VRAM 1.05, then 4.27; RAM swizzled 0.87, then 3.37) and 6.2
  unswizzled from RAM (2.03, then 12.6). Wide, per byte: about 2.9 (RAM swizzled), 14 (RAM unswizzled), 1.8-2.0 (VRAM).
  Round 6 measured VRAM (1.93 a byte) with a 256-wide sprite: the wide side. Killzone's and Activision Hits' CLUT32
  strips 32 texels wide take about 1.4 clocks a pixel, not about 8. The distinct texels are the fewer of the span and
  the texture's width: a 64-texel texture repeated over 256 pixels is narrow (`time-texcache`'s 64x64 swizzled 8888,
  0.92 a pixel).
- **Other textures** (`time-textures`): triangles aren't sprites: a 256x256 swizzled texture over 256x256 pixels in 3D
  takes 3.9 clocks a pixel, a 256-wide sprite of it 13.3 (sprites read along rows; triangles seem to go in blocks), the
  3D case drawn in perspective (case 13: w 1 at the left to 2 at the right, 0.5 to 2 texels a pixel across the screen).
  Unswizzled textures from RAM go by their size or row pitch (64x64, 16 KiB: 0.36 a byte; 512 wide, 1 MiB, narrow:
  1.73). Drawn wide (one sprite 512 texels across), a texture shrunk 2:1 costs about 1.9 times its 1:1 time a pixel, 4:1
  about 3.6 times, stretched 1:2 about half: about the square root of the texels a pixel. Read narrow it's more: in
  strips 64 texels wide (case 2) shrunk 2:1 takes 4.40 a pixel against 1.58 for 1:1 strips that wide, about 2.8 times
  (round 9 found about 3, part 110).
- **The front end** (`time-vertices`, `time-state`): a PRIM command about 60 clocks (one PRIM for each 8x8 sprite:
  95-98 clocks a sprite in `time-signals2`, each behind `sceGuGetMemory`'s JUMP over its vertices, 78-80 in
  `time-state`, their vertices in RAM; many sprites to a PRIM, round 6's time-sizes, 25); 0.5 a vertex's byte, but
  8-bit positions (3 bytes) 8.7 a vertex, more than floats' 5.9 (round 9: a floor of about 5); 35 an indexed vertex,
  with no cache of vertices (the same three again cost as much); a skinning weight about 6.5 a vertex; a point or spot
  light about 11; a directional light about nothing.
- **State** (`time-state`): TEX_FLUSH or a texture changed reloads a 1 KiB texture for about 374 clocks (unswizzled) or
  170 (swizzled), not round 6's 1444 and 614 (each 8x8 sprite reads 256 bytes of the 16x16 texture, which round 9's
  refetch rates, part 110, put at 343 to 374 unswizzled; the 170 isn't measured alone but inferred from case 6, below);
  a 256-color palette 252 (0.25 a byte); a matrix about 50; CALL and RET together about 58 (sprites drawn from CALLed
  lists against the same drawn directly); a blend or depth function, the alpha test, TEX_SYNC about nothing. Case 6's
  TEX_MODE costs 280 because GU's `sceGuTexMode` ends with a TEX_FLUSH (it jumps to `sceGuTexFlush`): that flush's
  reload, half swizzled and half not ((170 + 374) / 2); it says nothing of a TEX_MODE command alone.
- **Pixels** (`time-pixels`): the depth, alpha, stencil and color tests, blending and the texture functions add
  nothing beside a texture's fetching; a failing depth test still fetches. A cached texture, depth tested and blended,
  in full-width sprites (256 wide): 0.78-0.80 clocks a pixel into 8888, 0.34 into 5650; clear mode the same (the depth
  costs only in 32-bit). The rate goes by the primitive's size and shape, as the texels' does: `time-setup`'s 3D
  squares, textured and depth tested, drew their 8888 pixels at 0.38-0.39 a pixel at 16x16 (the same untextured),
  0.72-0.74 at 32x32 and 0.87-0.88 at 64x64; the 8x8 squares' 1.0 is their vertices' time (147 KB of float vertices a
  layer at round 9's 0.48 a byte, 1.08).
- **The SIGNAL** (`time-signals2`): when the back end keeps up, the finish comes a fixed 12 microseconds after the
  signal callback at 222 MHz (8 at 333: the callback's own CPU time); otherwise the front end gets at most about 28
  sprites of 64x64 or 20.5 triangles ahead: about 83 entries counting each primitive and each of its vertices (84.6 for
  sprites, 81.8 for triangles), not 16 primitives (part 106's provisional `GE::Cost::Queue`).
- **The scenes** (`time-scenes`): Killzone's scene list 12.4 ms at 222/111, its full-screen list 1.59 ms; the GE
  follows the bus's clock alone (333/222/166 as 333/166).
- **The CPU beside the GE** (`cpu-contention`): a CPU thread reading RAM makes the GE's layers textured from RAM take
  2.12 times as long (from VRAM 151 ms with the reader, against about 159 ms from `time-strips`' wide VRAM rate:
  there's no VRAM case without it); the GE drawing from RAM slows the CPU's reads of RAM by 26%
  (streaming) and 67% (a chain of pointers).
- **The two ends' overlap** (`time-overlap`): its two kinds of piece came out 14 to 1, not about as long as each other:
  at 222/111 the front-end pieces alone took 13.2 ms, the back-end ones 0.95; in turn 13.6 ms (1 or 16 at a time) and
  14.1 (256 at a time). Lopsided as they are, they overlap: taken in turn 1 or 16 at a time, 58 to 60% of the back end's
  time is hidden under the front end's (5 to 6% at 256 at a time); a balanced version is for a later round.
- **`time-lists`' stalls**: a fault of the program's, over a driver rule Phobos doesn't keep. Case 3 waits for
  `sceGeListSync(id, 1)` to say 3 (the GE has reached the stall address) before each move; uOFW's driver says 3 only
  when the stall address as the program gave it equals the GE's list address, which it keeps with the top three bits
  cut, and the program gave the uncached mirror's (0x4...), so it never did. The run's 5 seconds count from its start:
  the first wait used them all and the rest of the moves came at once, and `awaitFinishes`, on the same budget, then had
  no time left while the GE was still drawing those pieces (`sceGeDrawSync(1)` gave 2), so the program reported a stall.
  The GE never stalled: the note's 5000 ms is the run's whole budget, not 5 s a piece, and `sceGuBreak`'s 0x80000020
  (already: no list active) says the list had ended by the reset. After three such runs `timeCases8` gave up on the
  test: 67 of its 80 records are empty (case 3 at 4, 16 and 64 pieces, case 4, and every case at 333/166, 333/222/166
  and 266/133); the 13 that finished are 222/111's cases 0 to 2 and case 3's single piece. The program now gives cached
  addresses (`ge.c`'s `pieceEnds`; `pspmeasure.elf` rebuilt), and round 9's `time-lists2` (#276, part 110), the same
  cases with the fix, finished all 80 records at all four settings on his PSP: no run of round 8's `time-lists` again is
  needed. Phobos masks both addresses and says 3 there, so the core ran case 3 through; keeping the address as given is
  a small kernel change of its own, with a test, apart from this part.
- **The display as a program starts** (`display-start`, for part 108): the frame buffer reads address 0, width 0,
  format 3 (8888), for the next vblank and at once alike, and `sceDisplayIsForeground` 0. From there (put back before
  each try): 512 wide in 8888 or in 5650 at once, 0x80000107; the start's width and format with VRAM's address at
  once, 0x80000104; 0, 0, 0 at once, 0x80000107; 512 in 8888 for the next vblank, 0, after which the width reads 512 at
  once and the address 0 until the vblank.
- **The CPU's clocks** (`cpu-clocks`; noted only: the CPU's timing is a project of its own): the CPU's speed follows its
  own clock exactly (a loop 13.7 ms at 333 MHz, 20.6 at 222, 24.1 at 189, 45.8 at 99); granted 333/222/166 (read back as
  221/166), 266/133 (265/133) and 190/95 (189/95). The bus is granted at half the PLL, whatever is asked: 333/333/111
  gave 333/166 and 300/300/150 gave 299/166, and `scePowerSetBusClockFrequency(111)` and `(133)` from 333/166 returned 0
  with the bus left at 165: uOFW's `scePowerSetBusClockFrequency` refuses a bus above half the PLL (0x800001FE: `(166)`
  from 222/111, as `scePowerSetCpuClockFrequency(333)` there) and for a user-level caller sets the bus to half the PLL
  whatever was asked. Phobos's power service should do the same (part 104's rule covers only the refusals).
- **The CPU's own time** (noted for that project; 333/166, each test's median): an addition a cycle, dependent or not,
  as are loads that don't depend on each other; a load from the address the last one loaded, or a store, about 3; a
  taken branch with its delay slot, or a load used by the next instruction, about 4. A chain of pointers takes 5 cycles
  a step within 16 KiB (the data cache; with its loop's branch and add, the load alone being `cpu-alu`'s 3) and 73 (219
  ns) over 32 KiB to 8 MiB alike (no second cache); through RAM's uncached addresses 55 to 58, in the scratchpad 5, in
  VRAM 44 (37 uncached). Calls: `sceKernelGetSystemTimeLow` 0.56 microseconds, a semaphore's signal and poll 2.3,
  `sceKernelDelayThread(0)` 120, a thread switch there and back 19, `sceKernelDcacheWritebackAll` 10.6,
  `sceGeListEnQueue` about 14 (about 4,650 cycles: round 6's 5,200 from its return), `sceGeListUpdateStallAddr` with the
  list left waiting 0.53, `sceGeDrawSync(1)` 0.67, `sceDisplaySetFrameBuf` 0.95. `cpu-latency` and the other clocks are
  kept for that project.

The fit of the GE timing's model to rounds 6 and 8 (`tools/psp-measure/ge-terms.py` and `ge-fit.py`) and the model it
changes are part 106's, on #269; a `measured8` test, the core's run of round 8 beside these files, needs both this
program and that model, and comes once both are in.

## Part 108: the display's frame buffer for the next vertical sync — sceDisplaySetFrameBuf's sync 1 shown from the sync, sceDisplayGetFrameBuf answering for the one asked (Army of Two's 30/20 frames a second)

On branch `cursor/psp-display-latch-2b67` (draft PR #271), from master `5442acb8b` (part 102, #265; #264, no part),
masters `03eca2a69` (#274, no part), `dd63f4ffb` (parts 103 and 104, #266 and #267), `230c0a731` (part 105, #268)
and `92eddbfea` (part 109, #272; #273, no part) merged in. Sources: pspautotests' display/setframebuf and
display/isstate (their recordings), round 8's display-start (part 107, #270: `tools/psp-measure/cpu.c`), pspsdk's
`pspdisplay.h`. No PPSSPP or JPCSP. Save states: layout 33 (its own: #269's GE timing takes 33 too, and whichever
lands second renumbers its layout to 34).

### Why

- Army of Two (part 103's captures ULUS10472-1 and -2): each frame its list's SIGNAL callback sets the next frame
  buffer for the next vertical sync; after its draw sync the game asks `sceDisplayGetFrameBuf` which is shown (0),
  and while it isn't the new one yet, sets it again and waits for the blank: two flips and one wait a frame, 30
  frames a second while the GE's frame fits two blanks, 20 above, on the owner's PSP. Phobos took every frame buffer
  at once, so the game found its flip shown and never waited: master draws 251 frames a second (the GE timing
  "Fast") for 60 shown, part 106's PSP timing 29 to 32 a second with no cap.

### What a PSP does

- display/setframebuf: a frame buffer set with sync 1 (pspsdk's NEXTVSYNC) reads at once as the one coming
  (`sceDisplayGetFrameBuf`'s 1) and as the one shown (0) only from the next blank (read after
  `sceDisplayWaitVblankStart`); its width and format read at once from both. display/isstate: a frame buffer of 0 so
  set leaves the display in the foreground till then, and the vertical sync comes 631.5 microseconds into the blank.
  Round 8's display-start, from a program's start: one set for the next vblank (512 wide, 8888) is taken and reads
  back at once as address 0 (the start's), width 512 and format 3, the address the new one only from the blank.
- Five of the scenes below set theirs with sync 1 just as a blank starts (from a vertical blank handler, or a thread
  that waited for the blank): if the frame buffer were taken at the blank's start, each of their frames would show a
  blank late. Set in a blank before its sync, here they're taken at that sync, for the frame after the blank; set
  anywhere else, at the next blank's start, as setframebuf read it.
- (Also recorded, left out here for scope: refusals of a sync other than 0 and 1, of a width or format set at once
  that isn't the one shown (0x80000107), of widths not a multiple of 64 (0x80000104), formats past 3 (0x80000108) and
  addresses misaligned or outside VRAM and RAM (0x80000103). Round 8's display-start has what a program meets as it
  starts: address 0, width 0 and format 3 (8888) for the next vblank and at once alike, `sceDisplayIsForeground` 0,
  and every frame buffer set at once refused from there, the display left as it was (512 wide in 8888 or in 5650,
  and 0, 0, 0: 0x80000107; the start's width of 0 with VRAM's address: 0x80000104). Phobos starts at format 0 and
  takes every one. The refusals, and the start's format, change what every game meets as it starts: a change of
  their own, with a library check of its own (below, "Not yet").)

### What changed

- display.cpp: `sceDisplaySetFrameBuf`'s sync 1 sets the address shown from the next blank's start, or, set in a
  blank before its sync, from that sync (`Display::nextFrameBuffer`, `nextAt`; `Kernel::VsyncCycles`), the width and
  format at once; sync 0 (anything else) as before, replacing one waiting. `latchFrameBuffer()` makes it the one
  shown once its sync has come, as `sceDisplayGetFrameBuf` and `sceDisplayIsForeground` read, as another is set for
  the sync, and as each blank goes by (so a state saved as a frame starts is the same whether the game read it or
  not); `sceDisplayGetFrameBuf`'s which 1 reads the one coming. The screen (`presentedFrameBuffer()`:
  `Kernel::picture()`, system.cpp) shows in the frame after a blank the frame buffer its sync takes: the last one set,
  as before. Its picture is taken as the blank starts (`System::run()`), so one set in the blank before its sync,
  after that, shows a frame later than on a PSP, as on master.
- Save states: layout 33 keeps one waiting and its sync (13 bytes); older layouts load with none; a state with one
  due past the next blank's start is refused.

### What it does

- Every scene of both libraries (34, `cpu-round3/scenes` and `psp-hires/scenes`), the bench runners against master,
  100 frames from each state, in Software, Vulkan and Vulkan-fast: 31 the same as master in every frame's picture
  and VRAM and the RAM after, in all three. Three change, the same way in all three renderers:
  - Army of Two's gameplay and menu: every frame, and the RAM: its pacing (below).
  - Death Jr. II's character screen: every frame's picture the same; the VRAM in alternate frames (50 of 100) and
    the RAM: its vertical blank handler flips for the sync as the blank starts and reads which is shown, once on
    master; its reads before the sync find the old one now, so it reads twice more (the last at the next blank,
    which finds it), and its main thread, which never reads it on master, reads it five times before the sync. Its
    work around the flip changes with them, at 30 flips a second still, no blank waited for. (Its gameplay scene
    comes out the same in its 100 frames: its main thread reads once a flip, mid-frame, after the sync.)
- The first try (`latch/`: every frame buffer set for the sync taken at the next blank's start, the screen showing
  the one taken) changed four more, their flips at a blank's start each shown a blank late, in alternate frames:
