## Part 109: the GE's front end on a thread of its own, exact — option "GE Thread" (Off, the default, and On), the emulation thread waiting only where the GE could still change what it reads (GE round 4, part B, first PR)

On branch `cursor/psp-ge-thread-2b67`, on master `a8d5640f5` (part 101, #263) with masters `684ce8561` (#261, #262,
#249), `a8d5640f5`, `5442acb8b` (#264, the PGD layer's comments, #265: part 102), `03eca2a69` (#274), `a014706e9`
(#266: part 103), `dd63f4ffb` (#267: part 104) and `230c0a731` (#268: part 105) merged in. The design is GE round
4's (part 100 was its part A), revision 4, approved by the independent review with two conditions, both met (below).
Clean room: no PPSSPP for any GE or GPU code (its threaded GPU code included), JPCSP never. Save states: unchanged
(StateVersion as before; a state is the same file with the thread on or off).

**What it is.** With "GE Thread" On, the kernel's GE on the emulation thread (E) still runs every display list's
commands as it always has (the control pass: every word, JUMP and CALL, SIGNAL, FINISH and END, bounding boxes, block
transfers), and hands what draws to a second GE, the render GE, on a thread of its own (G), as records in a ring:
the state words with their addresses, each PRIM, curved surface and palette with the bytes it reads copied as of its
place, the CPU's writes the GE hears of, and the reads where G's memory may be busy. G draws them with the renderer and
the drawing threads, in the same memory seen through a view of its own, and makes the checks the synchronous GE makes
(its finishes, the drawing first over what it reads) where they come in the stream. Every emulated result is the
synchronous GE's, by construction:
- **The value rule** (`ge/model.hpp`): E keeps a model of what each PRIM handed over may change (where it may draw on
  the GPU and in software, its depth's 16 KiBs, the put points where a depth goes back into memory, above 1x each
  target's hull since its last finish) and of what G reports done (finishes, depth put back, software pixels drawn).
  A CPU load, an HLE function's copy out of VRAM and the control pass's reads of lists, vertices and palettes wait
  for G only where it may still change the bytes; elsewhere they read memory at once.
- **Versions** (`ge/versions.hpp`): E's writes (the CPU's stores reaching VRAM or a watched page, HLE functions'
  copies and fills, block transfers' rows) are made at once and handed over; their old bytes are kept as versions
  where G may still read them or write them back as of an earlier place, and G reads and writes back through them
  (it never waits while it holds a page: R13). A write over pixels the drawing threads may still draw, or onto a
  texture they may still read, goes after its record, once G has passed it.
- **The clock** (`kernel/ge.cpp`): no wait at a kick's end; the runs G counts are folded into the GE's time
  (`geFold()`), and a go limited by the time's bound is worked out exactly before anything sees it.
- **Debug checks**, on in every threaded test machine (and with `PHOBOS_GE_CHECK=1`): G runs E's model on the same
  records and aborts where a finish or a depth put-back changes a byte E may have read clean (the whole rule), or
  where G reads memory outside what the model declares the PRIM may read (G-interest: its target's rows, the rows of
  every target with pages there (R19), its depth's 16 KiBs to the most rows any target drew with it (R24) and the
  targets over them (R22), its texture's bytes, a put point's depth buffers).

**The option.** "GE Thread", Off (the default) or On, the core's option (`system.cpp`) and the runner's `--ge-thread`;
the app doesn't offer it yet. Part 103's GE profile (`--ge-profile`) records the same with the thread On: while it
records, each run handed over is counted at once and its charge recorded where the synchronous GE records it
(`Kernel::geProfiledRun()`), the threads taking turns at each run meanwhile. Part 105's skips through a game's polls of
the GE's looks (`sceGeListSync(id, 1)`, `sceGeDrawSync(1)`) hold with the thread On as they are: a look reads the
kernel's lists, which the control pass keeps on E as it always has, and what the GE thread decides is only when a FINISH
falls due; a skip ends before the go's limit, which is no later than the GE time's bound where the FINISH may come next
(`untilNextEvent()`), and makes sure by that bound that no FINISH falls due in it (`spinSkip()`), so it skips no further
than without the thread, at times fewer turns (the GE thread not done counting), which is exact. A test holds the GE
thread back at every step while a game polls each look, and every step's state is that of a machine without the thread
running every turn. **The limit of this first part**: the frame is still shown from the emulation thread, which drains G
at every frame's end (`System::run()`'s `ge.drawer()`), so the two threads overlap within a frame and not across frames;
showing the frame from G (every GPU call there, at most two frames in flight), the bounded drains and unloading with G
stuck (R10, R18), and Auto with its handover both ways (R17) are the second part's (design steps 3 and 4), which the
app's option waits for.

**Speed, in this first part**: On is exact, but on the M1 it's seldom faster than Off and in some games much slower
(the library's slowest with the software renderer, all 3,600 frames from their start, Off then On: BlazBlue 4 s and
20 s, SSX on Tour 8 s and 43 s, Aces of War 10 s and 41 s). Every CPU load and store reaching VRAM takes the slow path
(VRAM is out of E's page table all the while) and each store is a record of its own, G woken for it, about a
microsecond each: the design's access records only on pages where checks could act, with runs encoded as one record
(costed there at 5 ns a record), aren't done yet. And a game that touches what G is still drawing, or reads
the frame back, has the two threads take turns, the frame's end draining G. Auto keeps such a game synchronous;
until then On is for the tests and the runner.

**Off costs nothing.** Every Off path is master's (or the stage's own arithmetic, measured): the emulation thread's
retired instructions a frame against master on the M1, Vulkan fast, late frames as the app shows them, 300 frames,
5 rounds alternating: Super Monkey Ball's story -0.29% (ms -2.4%), Ghost of Sparta's menu -0.02% (ms +0.7%), Chains of
Olympus +0.05% (ms +0.2%; over 14 rounds interleaved +0.04%, master's own rounds spanning 0.45%). Getting there took
the Off paths back to master's text where the first 2c tree cost +0.40% on Ghost of Sparta: `Memory::changed()`'s
helpers inline again, `pieces()` inside `copyIn()` and `fill()` again, `pointerElsewhere()`'s `bool load`, a Look as
it was (the deferred decode's place kept by its batch), `transfer()`'s overwrite master's lambda, and stage 1's
`geReached()` and `idle()` folding nothing with no runs handed over. The review's fixes, against `0d7e04246` the same
way: -0.01%, -0.01%, -0.06%, once `geTime()`'s threaded branch was kept as it was, its fold of the oldest runs out of
line (`geFoldKept()`): written inline there it cost 0.19% in all three, `geTime()` being what every run takes.

**Exactness, measured** (the M1, MoltenVK; the thread On with both debug checks against Off on the same runner):
- the 78 settled hashes: the 26 scenes (the 21 of the kit, Hot Wheels, Killzone's play and menu, MX vs ATV, Chains of
  Olympus) in Vulkan fast, Software and Vulkan accurate, 100 frames, each frame's picture and VRAM with the drawing
  settled, then RAM and the machine's state: 78 of 78 the same;
- the 26 scenes 600 frames with only the end hashed and a state saved every 150 frames, each compared: all the same;
- Ghost of Sparta from its start with the library check's presses, 2,400 frames, each frame's picture and VRAM, then
  RAM and the state, in Software and Vulkan fast: the same (the clock started at a fixed time: a game booted takes
  the host's, which runs on between two runs);
- schedule fuzzing (`PHOBOS_GE_FUZZ=seed,mode,n`: G pausing before records; G held back till E has appended n more,
  waits for it, fills a quarter of the ring or 2 ms pass; E waiting for every record): 10 scenes three ways, 300
  frames, states every 100: all the same, none hung (every run under a hang timeout);
- the stress mode (a build with `PHOBOS_GE_STRESS_HOOK`; `PHOBOS_GE_STRESS=97`: the GPU finished at every kick's end
  and before every 97th PRIM, the same places with the thread or not; a scene's 101 finishes become 6,224): the 26
  scenes at 1x and 2x and eight at 4x: all the same;
- the suite: with the thread Off and On, and On fuzzed each of the three ways, 0 failures (604 groups now, with
  #265's and #266's merged in, the library check's two tests and the review's six; the delay fuzzing on the 590 before
  them); On under ThreadSanitizer with the GPU groups skipped, no report, nothing suppressed (the GPU groups under it:
  below).

**The targeted tests** (tests/psp/gpu.cpp and ge.cpp; each on an explicitly threaded machine, G held back by a test gate
where it would lag, against the same lists and accesses without the thread, both checks on; each fails with its rule
taken out): reads waiting only where G may change the bytes; stores waiting only for pixels the drawing threads may
still draw; deferred texture decodes read as of their own PRIMs; a transfer outside a list; the CPU's stores after a
list into a texture it draws; Ghost of Sparta's list copied into VRAM over drawn pixels and called there; a write
whose own checks finish the GPU (below); and the review's findings: R14 (a waited load leaves the GPU's pixels dirty),
R15 (halfword and byte stores into drawn pixels, each replayed alone), R16 (a depth of the other order taken through
memory), R19 (a move source's bytes beside its pixels before the drawer's rows), R22 (a depth fill reviving a source's
dead bytes on a page no rectangle reaches, after a long transfer row onto it), R23 (a depth put back over pixels a
finish put there since, at 1x and 2x, the moves on and off), R24 (a taller drawer's changed depth rows), and above 1x
the hull rule; and after the independent review: a store onto a texel a software PRIM reads but doesn't draw over,
software depth read through the depth views, a copy out of clean bytes on a block the GPU drew in, more runs than G
keeps counts of before a FINISH, reads of nothing reported, and the go split.

**Found on the way** (each with a test that fails without its fix):
- A write whose own record's checks finish the GPU (a store through VRAM's depth views onto a drawn pixel, a
  transfer's half pixels) with G caught up: the finish, before the write in the stream though G makes it after, put
  the drawn pixels back over it. The write's old bytes are now kept as a version wherever its pages may still be the
  GPU's, so the finish's write-back goes under it.
- R25, with the depth moves off (the fallback): a depth fill takes memory's bytes as they are where another target
  drew on the GPU since the last finish, and a later put writes that depth back over the pixels a finish has put there
  since, at 1x too, where the model's put rule held only above 1x. It holds now wherever a depth put back may not be
  memory's newest (above 1x, or the renderer's `depthMoves()` off).
- Found by ThreadSanitizer over the GPU groups (below): G starved while E writes into pages G writes back. E publishes
  a version, waits for G's pin to go, copies, makes it ready; G, finding an unready version on a page it pinned, let
  go and waited for it. With E writing on and on into such a page (pspsdk's samples, the CPU writing VRAM as the GPU
  finishes there), G saw each next version before its rescan ended, nothing freed while it was stuck on that record:
  quadratic, and under the sanitizer's slow atomics never done. Now E says it's copying once it has found the page
  unpinned, then looks at the pins again, and G waits only for a version being copied; one published under its pins,
  which waits for them, it reads past, memory having the bytes the copy will take (one of the two threads always sees
  the other's step: both store, then load, in one order). The R13 test's interleavings now include E stopped while
  copying (G waits) and E stopped after publishing till G is done (G goes on; the old protocol deadlocks there).
- Found by the coordinator's library check with the thread On (every game from its start, 3,600 frames; the pictures
  were Off's): two costs of the control pass that grew without bound. The textures the software renderer reads from
  memory as it draws were kept one entry per PRIM until drawn, and E went through them all at every report it took,
  which is at each load of VRAM, each list word read from VRAM and each vertex read, and at every write's look for a
  conflict: quadratic in the PRIMs G had yet to draw. Ghost of Sparta, its lists in VRAM, crawled past the check's 15
  minutes from its start (Off: 7), and Gran Turismo took 226 s (Off: 14). They're kept by page now, the newest PRIM
  over each, with nothing to go through (and the put points are dropped as a prefix: they come in their places'
  order): Gran Turismo 15 s. And an indexed PRIM's vertices were copied from the vertex address up to its most index,
  a byte at a time, so a big buffer's few vertices were copied whole for every PRIM (85% of E in Jeanne d'Arc); now
  from the least index to the most, in one copy from RAM: Jeanne d'Arc 123 s → 36 s (Off: 30). The tests: what the
  model keeps of the software textures in flight is as big with 8,000 software PRIMs behind as with 500 (kept by
  PRIM, the list every report went through grew by one entry each), and 20,000 loads of VRAM take less than four
  times as long with 8,000 behind as with 500, the best of three rounds each (15 times as long with the list kept by
  PRIM); and a sprite by indices 4000 and 4001 hands G a record no bigger than one by 0 and 1, which G reads as a run
  from the copy.
- Found by the independent review. Past 4,096 runs handed over before a FINISH is due (a GU direct list, its stall
  address moved at each draw, makes a run each), G's counts of later runs overwrote earlier ones' that E hadn't
  folded (runs fold only while a FINISH is due), a data race too: the GE's time came out wrong, and differently run
  to run. E now folds the oldest as each run past 4,096 is handed over (`Kernel::geTime()`; exact, the fold taking
  the cycles and the bus's clock kept at the hand-over). G's memory reported no read of nothing, so a texture where
  nothing is left the count a state keeps (`System::unmappedReports`) short of Off's by the software renderer's texel
  reads: G's memory reports through E's now, the count atomic and saturating at 16 (the drawing threads report too,
  with the thread off as well). Three rules no test caught (each taken out, the suites passed with the thread On)
  have tests now: the software textures' conflicts, page by page; the software depth rectangles; and the busy check
  made for a read whose page is busy but whose bytes are clean (an HLE copy out of VRAM's depth views, whose check
  covers the whole 16 KiB block and finishes the GPU wherever it drew there). And a write straddling two pages looks
  at both for a watched texture (an HLE write may).

**ThreadSanitizer and the GPU.** MoltenVK runs under ThreadSanitizer, nothing suppressed: every GPU group with the
thread On, pspsdk's samples included, the GE-thread groups and the versions' group: 0 failures, no report (78, 12 and
1 groups after the review's fixes, B1's fold and S1's reports among what they ran). Its first run, with the
samples left out, found one race, in the tests (a test gate set while G was still taking records and reading it:
the tests now drain the thread before setting it), none in the emulator, the render GE driving the GPU backend
included; its run with the samples found the starvation above.

**The go split is needed.** A go stopped at the GE time's bound runs on from where it stopped, with none of the run
loop's steps between, and the review found the case that needs it (the design's R5): a call into the program held
back while interrupts are off (an alarm gone off), the program turning them on with mtic, no system call, so the go
goes on, inside a go whose limit came from the bound. Ended at the bound, the loop's startCall() would start the call
there, at count 9,791 where the synchronous GE starts it at 19,583, with either engine. A test has it now, and fails
with the split taken out (the suite and the scenes didn't).

**Next (the second PR, stacked):** design steps 3 and 4: the frame shown from G (`Present` records, at most two
frames in flight, `Shot` and `Settings` records, the window handed over through G), the drains bounded and unloading
with G stuck, then Auto and its handover both ways, with switches forced at seeded frames.

## Part 110: psp-measure round 9 — triangles reading narrow textures, a texture's loads and the cache's reuse, vertex formats, time-lists again

On branch `cursor/psp-measure-round9-2b67` (PR #276), on master `14e8065dc` (#270, part 107: round 8, its results
and `time-lists`' fix; this branch was stacked on #270 until it merged). Round 9 of `tools/psp-measure`, for the owner's
PSP: what the fit of rounds 6 and 8 (#269, part 106) still guesses where its gate misses. Nothing in the core changes:
the program, its test, the test programs' copy of it. Clean room as part 107: our own code; pspsdk's headers and
uOFW's reading of the driver; no PPSSPP or JPCSP.

### Where the gate misses, and what the model guesses there

#269 is held until every captured scene is within 15% of the owner's PSP-1000, none more than 15% too slow; 5 of its
9 judged rows pass (part 106). The four that don't, and the model's guesses round 9 measures:

- **Super Monkey Ball Adventure's story, −31%** (its copy in round 8, `time-scenes` 5, −24%): its 200 CALLed lists
  each set a 16 KiB CLUT8 texture and load its palette. Round 8's `time-textures` 19 to 24 had a texture of its own
  for each 32x32 sprite cost the PSP about the same a sprite whether it was 1, 4 or 16 KiB (7.4 microseconds at
  222/111, about 820 bus clocks), where the model loads a texture of 8 KiB or less whole, by its size. Its figures
  follow the texels a sprite touches instead: 512 bytes (CLUT4) 590 clocks, 1 KiB (CLUT8, any size of texture) 820,
  2 KiB (5650) 1,330, so about half a clock a byte touched over some 350 for the sprite itself; and `time-state` had
  the same texture set again cost as much as another (TEX_FLUSH reloads it): about 390 clocks for each 8x8 sprite's
  8x8 texels, 256 bytes, of an unswizzled 16x16 texture.
- **Ghost of Sparta's main menu, −21%, and Killzone's second capture, −19%**: longer in the game than round 8's copies
  of them alone, the more they read from RAM (round 8's `cpu-contention`: a thread reading RAM makes the GE's
  RAM-textured drawing 2.12 times as long): the CPU's timing, a project of its own. But both draw mostly triangles,
  and the model takes triangles reading narrow textures at a sprite's rates, never measured: round 8 had triangles
  only reading a 256x256 texture whole, in perspective (3.9 clocks a pixel, w 1 to 2, where a 256-wide sprite took
  13.3).
- **Activision Hits Remixed's 3D menu, +29% by the gate** (too slow): the gate takes the median over all of a scene's
  lists, which sets the PSP's 5.4 ms list (its third) beside Phobos's 7.0 ms one (its second): different lists. List
  for list (part 106's times: the PSP's 21.2, 3.5 and 5.4 ms, Phobos's 15.3, 7.0 and 3.5), the second list is +100%
  (3.5 ms on the PSP, 7.0 here: 434,000 pixels in 786 primitives), the third −35% and the first −28%, the frame −14%
  (30.1 against 25.8 ms); the gate's cross-list median is #269's to settle. The second list's copy in round 8 fits,
  so it's something of the game's list the model takes as dearer than it is: its triangles' texels are the model's
  guess too.
- **Vertices**: round 8's culled strips had 8-bit positions take 4.5 times the model's time and 16-bit 1.5 times
  (floats as fitted), the strips' corners falling a little differently in each format.
- **Lists**: round 8's `time-lists` left 67 of its 80 records empty, 13 finished, all at 222/111 (part 107: the
  driver says the GE has reached a stall address only when the address as given is the GE's own, which it keeps with
  its top three bits cut, and the program gave the uncached mirror's); #270's program gives cached ones, which round 9's
  `time-lists2` ran.

### What round 9 measures

A new first line of the menu, "Round 9: the GE's triangles, textures, vertices (about 0.1 MB)"; every other line is
one further down. Its timed lists are round 8's kind (`timeCases8`): built once a case and size, each queued alone
and timed from just before `sceGeListEnQueue` to the finish callback, every run kept, at 222/111 and 333/166 MHz;
`time-lists2` at all four of round 8's settings. `manifest9.txt` lists every case.

- **`time-anchors`**, first: 15 of round 8's cases built by round 8's own functions at its sizes: `time-strips` 2, 6,
  30, 37, 41 and 44 (VRAM 8888 strips 32 wide and one sprite 512 wide, RAM 8888 unswizzled 32 wide, swizzled 32 and
  512 wide, RAM CLUT8 32 wide), `time-textures` 13 and 19 (3D in perspective; a texture of its own for each sprite),
  `time-state` 0 and 1 (nothing, TEX_FLUSH between sprites), `time-vertices` 0 and 2 (culled strips, float and 8-bit
  positions), `time-pixels` 0 (the textured fill), `time-setup` 1 (16x16 squares) and `time-scenes` 0 (Killzone's
  scene list): this session's PSP beside round 8's (whose round 6 repeated within 0.15% at the median).
- **`time-tristrips`**: round 8's strips over the target's 512x256, texel for pixel from textures 512 texels wide, in
  strips 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 and 256 wide and all 512 at once, as triangles (two a strip, corner to corner) in through
  mode, from seven textures: RAM 8888 swizzled and not, VRAM 8888 swizzled and not, RAM CLUT8 512x256 swizzled, VRAM
  CLUT8 swizzled, RAM 5650 swizzled; sprites over the two swizzled VRAM textures (round 8's VRAM ones were all
  unswizzled); squares 8x8 to 64x64 of two triangles tiling the target, as a mesh draws a big texture (RAM 8888, VRAM
  8888, RAM CLUT8); strips 32 and 256 wide in 3D (identity matrices, w 1) beside through mode's; strips 32 wide
  bilinear, triangles and sprites; and strips 32 pixels wide shrinking the texture 2:1 onto 256x256, triangles and
  sprites (the model takes the square root of the texels a pixel). Its sprites' cases and round 8's give the same
  strips both ways, in one session or two (the anchors).
- **`time-loads`**: sprites, each its own PRIM, with something done before each: nothing (one texture), a new texture
  (sceGuTexImage: its address, buffer width, size and TEX_FLUSH), the same one set again, TEX_FLUSH alone, the address
  and buffer width alone without TEX_FLUSH (the same or a new one), two textures in turn either way. CLUT8 textures
  8x8 to 256x256 (64 bytes to 64 KiB) drawn whole or 32x32 texels of each, in sprites 8x8 to 128x128; 8888 swizzled
  and not, from RAM and VRAM, 5650, CLUT4 and CLUT8 unswizzled and in VRAM, new or set once; textures set, TEX_FLUSHes
  and palette loads with no sprite between (N of them, then one sprite); palettes of 16 to 256 colors loaded before
  each sprite, 8888, 5650 and from VRAM, and a new texture with its palette each time (Super Monkey Ball's lists);
  mipmaps in 3D: each square's own 32x32 texture at 1:1, against 64x64 ones with a 32x32 level, the level set to 1
  (does the GE load level 0 too?), shrunk 2:1 without the level and with it chosen, and one such texture set once.
- **`time-formats`**: the same triangles in every format, three vertices each, every vertex once (tiny triangles in
  32x32 cells of 4 pixels, their positions in whole units every format holds exactly: in 3D an 8-bit k, a 16-bit 256k,
  a float k/128, a pixel each; in through mode pixels). Culled in 3D: 8-bit, 16-bit and float positions alone and with
  an 8888 or 5650 color, texture coordinates or a normal of each width, and whole vertices (texture coordinates, color,
  normal, position) of 16-bit, float and 8-bit parts; through 16-bit indices, and 8-bit ones; drawn (culling off) in
  3D and in through mode; strips of 128 triangles with each width of position. A PSP takes 8-bit positions in through
  mode as 0 (pspautotests' `gpu/primitives` recorded it drawing their points at (0, 0); the core does the same, part
  33), so that case draws nothing: the front end alone.
- **`time-lists2`**: round 8's `time-lists` as #270 fixed it (stall addresses cached), every case at 222/111,
  333/166, 333/222/166 and 266/133: a list's own time (0 to 64 small sprites), 1 to 8 lists queued at once, a list
  drawn while its stall address is moved on 1 to 64 times, as fast as the CPU goes and each time once the GE has
  reached it, 16 to 1024 CALLs. Named anew, as a round skips a test whose file is there and the owner's `results/ge`
  keeps round 8's `time-lists.bin`.

### How it runs

- About a minute on the PSP, two at most: its lists are about 35 seconds of the GE's time by round 8's rates (sprites'
  rates for the triangle cases, an upper bound), with some 9,600 runs' own overhead and the lists' building (the
  vertex formats' 49,152 vertices the most); about 0.1 MB. It changes the clocks as round 8 does and puts them back
  after each test.
- The owner: copy `EBOOT.PBP` over the old one in `PSP/GAME/PSPMEASURE`, keeping `results/` (round 9's files are new
  names beside rounds 2 to 8's, none overwritten); ARK's clock settings at Auto; the charger in; the GE profiler
  plugin off (it times the same lists); run "Round 9" (the menu's first line); send `results/ge` back.
- A list the GE hasn't finished in 5 seconds is a stall (reset, recorded, the test goes on), as since round 4;
  `time-lists2`'s waits for the stall address are bounded the same way.

### The test

"psp measure" (tests/psp/measure.cpp) runs round 9 after round 8, through the menu (every line one further down), and
checks its five files as round 8's: whole records, as many as the tables give (time-anchors 66, time-tristrips 352,
time-loads 216, time-lists2 80, time-formats 204), each test's settings in turn with the clocks the core grants, every
run finished, time-lists2's third time no later than its finish; and `manifest9.txt`. The core's times are this
branch's GE timing (part 64's peaks), so they say nothing of the PSP's; they show the lists do what they say: every
strip, square and 3D strip case draws the target's 131,072 pixels (295 microseconds at 111 MHz), the mipmapped squares
their 1,024 pixels each, the culled vertex cases nothing, the drawn ones their primitives, the textures set and
palettes loaded with no sprite between nothing but their list, and `time-lists2` all four settings.

At 333/166 the same costs come out within about 5% in bus clocks, a few percent fewer (as part 76 found).

### What round 9 answers for the refit, and what it doesn't

No model changes here: the refit is #269's. Against the gate's rows that fail:

- **Super Monkey Ball Adventure, −31%: answered.** A texture costs the texels read after each TEX_FLUSH (rates
  above), not its size, and a palette load about 200 bus clocks a kilobyte; the model loads a texture of 8 KiB or
  less whole by its size (0.132 a byte swizzled from RAM: 3.5 times too little a byte), takes a bigger one by the
  square root of its texels a pixel, and a palette at 0.362 a byte once the queue has emptied. Round 8's copy of its
  lists (`time-scenes` 5, −24% in the model), 9.7 microseconds a CALLed list at 222/111 (1,078 bus clocks), comes to
  about 1,160 at round 9's rates: a new 32x32 texels' read and its palette 702, its 30 float vertices about 344, the
  PRIM, CALL and RET about 110.
- **Ghost of Sparta's main menu, −21%: candidates, not an answer.** Three of round 9's findings make the model too
  fast where they apply: a texture shrunk while read narrow costs 2.8 to 3.4 times a pixel at 2:1 (the model's square
  root, two), and Ghost of Sparta reads its 512x512 frame buffers at two texels a pixel; rows past about 140 texels
  read wide (the model's threshold is 256); and RAM-textured meshes share the RAM with their vertices (the model
  overlaps the two ends freely). Which of them its lists meet, and how far the CPU beside the GE (round 8's
  `cpu-contention`, not measured again) accounts for the rest, is for the refit with the scene's terms.
- **Activision Hits Remixed's 3D menu, +27 to +29% by the gate: list for list, its second list +100% (too slow), its
  first and third too fast, the frame −14%.** The gate's median sets the PSP's third list beside Phobos's second
  (above), and the capture at `ahr-menu`'s moment repeats it (+27%, the coordinator's reading by the gate's measure).
  For the second list's overcharge, round 9 rules out its triangles' narrow texels (a triangle reading narrow costs
  about a sprite's, which the model already charges) and finds the model's rates for triangles reading wide too low, not
  too high (1.37 a byte swizzled from RAM, 0.770 from VRAM, against about 2.8 and 1.9 measured at 512 wide). What's left
  to check in that list's terms: triangles the model takes as wide by their extent while their rows span fewer than
  about 140 texels (narrow on the PSP, a fifth to a third of the wide cost), and its textures' reuse (a 4 KiB texture
  set once costs 0.52 a pixel over 64x64 sprites, 0.87 refetched each time). The first and third lists, too fast here,
  may meet the Ghost of Sparta row's candidates.
- **Killzone's scene list** (24 to 35 ms across the level in the new captures, the coordinator's reading): not this
  round's. Its copy (round 8's `time-scenes` 0) repeats within 0.14% (its slope 0.12 to 0.14%); what changes across the
  level is what the game draws, so the gate wants the capture at `kz-gp`'s moment beside Phobos's state, the other
  moments shown as another moment.
- **Elsewhere in the model**: a vertex 0.48 a byte with a floor of 5 and 8.5 for 3 bytes (the model: 0.523 a byte,
  no floor); an indexed vertex 32.6 to 38.5 by size (the model's 35.7 holds); bilinear 10 to 25% (the model: none);
  through mode as 3D; a stall update costing nothing beyond its call; the front end's lead about 30 sprites, as the
  queue has it; the bus's clock alone.
- **Not answered**: the CPU's share in the RAM-heavy scenes; the texture cache's organization (only its size is
  bounded) and the row threshold more closely than 128 to about 145 texels; pixels drawn after an address changed
  without TEX_FLUSH (the timing says no refetch; no picture was saved); bilinear or mipmapped textures shrunk,
  perspective, CLUT4 wide.

### The fix round (#270's review)

#270's review (`~/phobos-work/scratch/review-270/REVIEW.md`, approve with should-fixes) left one change to the
program for this pull request, which carries `cpu.c` to the owner's PSP next (its should-fix 10), and two small
ones with it; #270's own fixes (part 107's account, comments) and master `fe3deab82` (parts 108 and 109) came in
with #270's head `502bd680a`.

- **`cpu.c`'s waits for the GE had no deadline**: `cpu-syscalls`' enqueue-and-sync case waited in
  `sceGeListSync(id, 0)`, its back-to-back case in `sceGeDrawSync(0)` and its stall cases' end in
  `sceGeListSync(id, 0)`, as long as the GE took. Each now looks (`sceGeListSync(id, 1)` or `sceGeDrawSync(1)`) till
  the list is done, `Patience` (5 s) at most, as every other wait since round 4; past it the GE is taken to have
  stalled: `cpu-syscalls.stalled` says so and the GE is reset by `ge.c`'s own path (`geReset`, shared through
  `measure.h` with the test's file, as `Patience` is), and the GE's cases record their remaining runs as not finished
  (0xffffffff), calling the GE no more. A look returns at once, so the timed case (an empty list queued, then its
  sync) costs what it did whenever the list is done by the first look, as an empty list is.

## Part 112: psp-measure round 10 — lights by kind, CLUT32 triangles, wide triangles into 16-bit, perspective and turned, mipmaps, narrow strips, the CPU beside the GE

On branch `cursor/psp-measure-round10-2b67` (PR #278), from master `d428d91f9` (#276, part 110: round 9 and its
results). Round 10 of `tools/psp-measure`, for the owner's PSP: the cases #269's refit with round 9 (`c0d9c14a2`, part
106) still misses, as its agent (1fd9133c) specified them from each failing scene's terms and a log of the PRIMs' state
as the games set it. The cases are synthetic: no game's lists, textures or vertices are in the program (`pspmeasure.elf`
is public), only the parameters the log shows (sizes, formats, filters, palette loads, light kinds and factors). Nothing
in the core changes: the program, its test, the test programs' copy of it. Clean room as part 107: our own code;
pspsdk's headers and uOFW's reading of the driver; no PPSSPP or JPCSP.

### Where the refit misses

- **Super Monkey Ball Adventure's story, −30%**: mostly the PSP's CPU competing with the GE for RAM: round 8's copy of
  its lists (time-scenes 5) is 9 to 13% short with the CPU idle. Killzone's courtyard (−12 to −14%, its copy within 0 to
  3%) and later moments (−14 to −34%), and the rest of Ghost of Sparta's menu's miss (−10.8%) and its later scenes
  (−17%, −20%), point the same way. Round 8's cpu-contention had one pattern (a thread reading RAM: the GE's
  RAM-textured layers 2.12 times as long, its VRAM-textured ones about the same).
- **Activision Hits Remixed's 3D menu, its first list −19%** (2.35 million bus clocks a list on the PSP, the refit's
  pipeline 1.90): bound by its front end in the model, its lights spotlights with their shine (specular), two a PRIM, on
  some PRIMs a directional light with its shine too. Round 8's time-vertices had one directional light with its shine
  cost 20.7 clocks a vertex (the model 1.49) but four 1.2 each, and no spot or point light with shine; round 6's four
  fading point lights with their shine (time-primitives 13) are 25.5% short.
- **Its second list, +56%** (3.48 ms on the PSP): 720 triangles reading a CLUT32 texture (512x512 in VRAM, the 8888
  buffer the first list drew) in tiles of 32x34 pixels, each drawn three times with the palette shifted and loaded
  again, into 5650. On the PSP the tiles' texels cost next to nothing, where the refit fetches each tile's 4,352 bytes;
  no round had timed CLUT32 in triangles.
- **Its copyright screen, its second list −24%**: its picture (CLUT8 512x256, RAM, swizzled) drawn twice as two 3D
  triangles over 480x272, bilinear and blended, into 5650, in about what one sprite of it takes (round 8's time-scenes
  2), where the refit, by round 9's rows, reads only 72% of a triangle's pixels wide. Round 9's two triangles drew into
  8888 (and fit that rule within 1%).
- **What the refit leaves out**: triangles in perspective (round 8's time-textures 13 to 15, round 6's time-fill 39:
  about half the time the refit gives the same at w 1), turned a quarter (time-textures 16 to 18: 39 to 53% over), a big
  texture's mipmaps (time-textures 10 to 12: 75 to 80% short), and 8-texel CLUT8 strips from VRAM (round 8's time-strips
  21, round 9's time-tristrips 35: −50%).

- **`time-contention`** (197): the CPU beside the GE. Ten lists, each at two sizes: A an 8888 512x512 texture (RAM,

  17 patterns: arithmetic alone (64 additions a turn); a line's 16 words read within 8 KiB (the data cache's hits); a
  line read streaming over 1 MiB (a miss each), flat out and slowed by an empty loop between lines to a half, a quarter
  and an eighth of that (the loop's turns measured as each clock setting begins); a line written streaming over 1 MiB
  (write-backs), flat out and a quarter; 64 KiB copied a turn (memcpy); a step of a chain of pointers 64 bytes apart
  over 1 MiB (one miss at a time); 16 words read through the uncached mirror; a line read, and one written, in VRAM's
  last 256 KiB through the cache; a game's mix (12 additions, 2 reads and 2 writes a turn at random words) over 16, 64
  and 256 KiB and 1 MiB. Each pattern alone for 10 ms too. A run's four words: the list's time to its finish callback
  and `sceGeListEnQueue`'s return (alone: the thread's 10 ms, 0), the thread's turns, and their time.
- **`time-contention2`** (54): the streaming reads, flat out and slowed, with each list and alone, at 333/222/166 (the
  CPU at 222 MHz with the bus at 166): the bus apart from the CPU's clock.

### How it runs

- About two minutes on the PSP, three at most: its lists are about 70 seconds of the GE's time by rounds 8 and 9's
  rates, with some 12,900 runs' own overhead and the lists' building; about 0.2 MB. It changes the clocks as round 8
  does and puts them back after each test.
- Its files are new names in `results/ge` beside rounds 2 to 9's, none overwritten (a test whose file is there is
  skipped, as ever).
- Every wait for the GE keeps to 5 seconds: a list not finished by then is a stall (recorded, the GE reset, the test
  goes on). The contention thread runs at a priority above the program's own (nothing of the program's runs between a
  list's start and its finish), started before the list is queued but waiting on a semaphore until it is, and stops
  itself at the finish callback's flag, at its 10 ms alone, or at 5 seconds whatever happens: it can't hold the PSP. Its
  memory is a 1 MiB array of its own and VRAM's last 256 KiB (which time-clut32's filled buffer runs 96 KiB into, at
  another time); what it wrote through the cache is written back and invalidated after each run, so no line of it lands
  later on anything else.
- The owner: copy `EBOOT.PBP` over the old one in `PSP/GAME/PSPMEASURE`, keeping `results/`; ARK's clock settings at
  Auto; the charger in; the GE profiler plugin off (it times the same lists); run "Round 10" (the menu's first line);
  send `results/ge` back.

"psp measure" (tests/psp/measure.cpp) runs round 10 after round 9, through the menu (every line one further down), and
checks its nine files as round 9's: whole records, as many as the tables give (time-anchors2 42, time-lights 230,
time-clut32 88, time-widetri 72, time-perspective 192, time-mipmaps 88, time-vram8 240, time-contention 754,
time-contention2 104 at 333/222/166 alone), each test's settings in turn with the clocks the core grants, every run
finished; the contention thread's turns and their time wherever it ran, and nothing where it didn't; and
`manifest10.txt`. The core's times are this branch's GE timing, so they say nothing of the PSP's.

- **Narrow strips** (`time-vram8`): a strip's row costs by the 16-byte units it touches. VRAM CLUT8 not swizzled,

  25.4: 16 wide the cheapest); CLUT4 0.80 down to 0.60 (32 texels a unit); swizzled VRAM 28 to 37% cheaper (CLUT4 15 to
  19%); triangles 1.5 to 1.8 times the sprites at these widths in VRAM CLUT8 (VRAM CLUT4 1.3 to 1.7, RAM CLUT8 1.1 to
  1.3). Round 8's case 21 again 1.54. The −50% case (8 wide) pays a whole unit's row for half its texels.
- **The CPU beside the GE** (`time-contention`, `time-contention2`), the GE's time beside each pattern against alone
  (the larger size):
  - CPU work without RAM traffic (arithmetic, the data cache's hits) doesn't slow the GE (×0.97 to 1.01). RAM traffic
    slows every list that reads RAM; VRAM-only lists (VRAM-textured, untextured) not at all (×1.00 to 1.01), but by the
    CPU's own VRAM reads and writes (×1.5 to 2.5).
  - By what the GE reads (beside streaming reads / writes / a chain of pointers / a game's mix over 64 KiB or more):
    wide RAM texels ×1.85 / 2.74 / 3.21 / 2.95; Super Monkey Ball's CALLed lists ×1.38 / 1.52 / 1.71 / 1.54; its small
    trilinear strips ×1.31 / 1.44 / 1.55 / 1.47; a new texture each sprite ×1.45 / 1.61 / 1.84 / 1.66; RAM-to-VRAM
    copies ×1.48 / 1.60 / 1.96 / 1.67; vertices and list words (NOPs) ×1.38 to 1.40 / 1.30 to 1.32 / 1.38 to 1.42 / 1.30
    to 1.32; Ghost of Sparta's kind (skinned, lit: its front end's) ×1.10 / 1.11 / 1.15 / 1.12. Copies and uncached
    reads as writes and chains; the mix over 16 KiB (mostly hits) ×1.03 to 1.25.
  - In proportion to the CPU's traffic, a little above: streaming reads at a half, a quarter and an eighth of flat out
    make wide RAM texels ×1.65, 1.30, 1.16 and Super Monkey Ball's lists ×1.26, 1.14, 1.07.
  - The CPU slowed in turn: streaming reads keep 0.42 to 0.78 of their rate alone (least beside vertices and list
    words), uncached reads 0.14 to 0.32, a chain 0.28 to 0.69, the mix 0.19 to 0.54.
  - At 333/166 the same ratios within a few percent; at 333/222/166 every list alone takes what it does at 333/166
    (within 1%: the bus's clock), and streaming reads flat out slow them as much (wide RAM texels ×1.91, the lists
    ×1.39), while the CPU's own streaming rate sits between (1.52 turns a microsecond, 1.34 at 222/111, 2.02 at
    333/166).

### What round 10 answers for the refit, and what it doesn't

For #269's agent (1fd9133c) to fit; no model change here.

- **Activision Hits' menu, its first list (−19%)**: a light's shine costs about 8 clocks a light-vertex on spot and
  point lights (19.0 against 11.0; 11 for a lone one), as the spec's 7 guessed, and about 2 on a directional light
  beside them; directional lights alone shine for about 1. The refit's one SpecularLight term wants splitting by kind,
  with point and spot lights' cost the same and their parameters free. Round 8's case 22 (20.7) is out of the fit as a
  state artifact.
- **Its second list (+56%)**: CLUT32 fetches as 8888 does, and a buffer just drawn reads no cheaper; the logged tiles
  alone take 3.23 of the game's whole list's 3.48 ms on the PSP, leaving almost nothing for its sprites, so the miss is
  in what the log says the list draws, for the log to settle.
- **Its copyright screen (−24%)**: bilinear reading wide costs 20% more, which the refit doesn't charge; the 16-bit
  target changes nothing, and the triangles' share of a sprite holds (77% bilinear, 79 to 80% nearest).
- **Perspective**: a row reads wide by how its texture coordinates step, not by the triangle's extent: w changing along
  a row takes a wide row from 10.0 clocks a pixel to 4.2 to 6.2 (narrow rows don't change); w constant, or changing down
  the screen, keeps it wide. Turned rows read wide past 64 to 128 texels down a column.
- **Mipmaps**: the wide rule goes by level 0's span; the filter's cost is bilinear's 20%, a blend of levels nothing;
  Super Monkey Ball's small strips are their vertices' and PRIMs'.
- **Narrow strips**: a row costs by its 16-byte units touched, about 11 to 15 clocks one, 18 to 25 two (VRAM CLUT8), not
  by its bytes.
- **The CPU beside the GE**: the slowdown is by the kind of GE read, 1 + K at a streaming reader (u = 1): K about 0.85
  for wide RAM texels, 0.4 for list words and vertices, 0.3 to 0.5 for small textured strips, texture loads and copies,
  0.1 for Ghost of Sparta's front-end-bound strips, 0 for VRAM-only work; roughly linear in the CPU's traffic; a game's
  mix over 64 KiB or more as a streaming reader or more (×1.3 to 1.7, wide texels ×3). The spec's prototype K of 0.56
  and round 8's 1.12 bracket these by kind. The CPU's own rate falls to a fifth to three quarters beside the GE.
- **Placement**: a swizzled RAM texture 64 bytes off a 128-byte boundary costs 7% more, a 1 KiB palette 6 to 20%; other
  placements move RAM reads by up to 26% either way. A fit across rounds should take each run's places into account, or
  weight the cases that don't read RAM.

### Round 10b: polling, before and beside, and placement

A top-up the owner runs the same night, as #269's agent specified it for the refit
(`~/phobos-work/scratch/psp-ge-profile/round10/SPECS-10b-1fd9133c.md`): the two CPU patterns that came after round 10
was built, and placement as a case of its own. Its own menu line (the first: "Round 10b: the CPU polling, before and
beside; placement"), its own files and `manifest10b.txt` (nothing of round 10's touched), round 10's framework and
safety. From this build on the arrays the GE reads (`big`, `bytes8`, `palette`, `timed`, `texture`, `texture16`,
`contendRegion`) are on 1 KiB boundaries, so its swizzled RAM textures don't carry round 10's 7%.

- **`time-contention3`** (48 cases): round 10's time-contention (`runContention10`, its thread above the program's
  priority released after the enqueue) with six of its lists (A wide RAM texels, C untextured, D vertices, E2 Super
  Monkey Ball's lists, H its small trilinear strips, I Ghost of Sparta's kind) at the same sizes, against six patterns:
  polling, a turn being `sceKernelPollSema` on a semaphore nothing signals, `sceGeListSync(the list, 1)` or
  `sceGeDrawSync(1)`, each with `sceKernelGetSystemTimeLow` (busy, but in the cache's or the kernel's; the deadline
  looked at every turn); 1 MiB written (16384 lines) by the program before it queues the list at once, the same with
  `sceKernelDcacheWritebackAll` between (the dirty lines landed before the GE starts), and by the thread once beside the
  list, then stopping. Each pattern alone first (the polls for 10 ms, the writes once), then each list alone and beside
  each, as time-contention's layout (the first list's case 6, rows of 7). The writes before a list give 16384 and their
  microseconds in the thread's words' place.
- **`time-placement`** (14): round 8's time-strips 37 strips (RAM 8888 512x512 swizzled, 32 wide) with the texture 0,
  16, 32, 64, 96, 128 and 512 bytes past a 1 KiB boundary; not swizzled at 0 and 64; RAM CLUT8 512x256 swizzled at 0 and
  64; a 1 KiB palette loaded before each 32x32 sprite (round 9's time-loads 45) at 0 and 64; and time-clut32's tiles
  once over from a CLUT32 texture swizzled in RAM (the spec's optional line: no round had it).
- About half a minute of the GE's time at 222/111 and 333/166, 9,000 or so runs; about 30 KB. The same safety as round
  10's: new names, the clocks put back after each test, every GE wait 5 s with the reset, the thread's own 5 s deadline
  (and the writer's 16384 lines), its writes written back and invalidated after each run.
- "psp measure" runs round 10b after round 10 (every menu line one further down) and checks its two files
  (time-contention3 180 records, time-placement 56) and `manifest10b.txt`, the thread's turns where it ran and none
  where it didn't, and the writes before a list their 16384.


### Round 10b's results (the owner's run, 2026-10-18 night)

The owner ran round 10b (EBOOT `6fa4ca80…`, `2578e331a`'s program) the same night; the coordinator pulled it at 20:23
(`~/phobos-work/scratch/psp-ge-profile/results-r10b`: `time-contention3.bin`, `time-placement.bin`, `manifest10b.txt`,
each one's sha256 the device's), nothing stalled, every run finished, 180 and 56 records as the tables give. Decoded
here (`r10.py`); #278's review decoded it too and agrees with every figure below.

- **Polling doesn't slow the GE.** Beside each of the six lists, at both sizes and clocks, a CPU polling through
  `sceKernelPollSema`, `sceGeListSync(the list, 1)` or `sceGeDrawSync(1)` (each turn with `sceKernelGetSystemTimeLow`
  and the deadline's look: 2.6 to 3.5 µs a turn at 222/111) leaves the list ×0.97 to 1.03 of its time alone: a polling
  CPU's busy time isn't RAM traffic.
- **Nor does work before the list.** 1 MiB written by the program (9.1 ms at 222/111, 6.0 at 333/166) just before it
  queues the list leaves the list ×0.99 to 1.05 (the 1.05 the small strips' smaller size), with the cache written back
  first ×1.00 to 1.03: the dirty lines landing late cost little, and only the work beside the GE counts.
- **Beside it, once: the writer outran every list.** The thread looked at the clock each turn (a system call), so it
  wrote 0.64 lines a microsecond at 222/111 and 0.94 at 333/166 (alone it reached its 10 ms at 6,376 and 9,347 lines);
  its megabyte would take about 26 and 17 ms, longer than every list, so it overlapped each one whole: a writer at about
  half round 10's flat-out writes' rate (1.21 and 1.80 lines a microsecond). Beside it wide RAM texels took ×2.00 to
  2.14 (round 10: ×2.74 flat out, ×1.48 at a quarter), Super Monkey Ball's lists ×1.36 to 1.37, vertices ×1.30 to 1.33,
  its small strips ×1.27 to 1.28, Ghost of Sparta's kind ×1.07, untextured ×1.00: the slowdown by the writer's rate, as
  round 10 found. A burst over part of a list, the spec's f, is still to be measured.
- **Placement** (one layer of round 8's time-strips 37 strips, against the texture on a 1 KiB boundary: 2,163.5 µs,
  within 0.4% of round 10's own case on one): 16, 32, 64 and 96 bytes past cost 6.7, 6.4, 5.6 and 7.3% more at 222/111
  (7.4 to 7.7% at 333/166), 128 and 512 past 2.1 and 1.5% (1.75 and 1.4%): an offset that isn't a multiple of 128 bytes
  costs 6 to 8%, a multiple of 128 off a 1 KiB boundary 1.5 to 2%. Not swizzled, 64 past costs nothing (−0.03%, −0.18%);
  swizzled CLUT8 64 past 5.1% (5.9%); a 1 KiB palette 64 past 5.7% (5.3%: 526 against 498 clocks a sprite). CLUT32
  swizzled in RAM, the tiles once over: 2,841 µs, 2.42 clocks a pixel (VRAM not swizzled 1.74, RAM not swizzled 8.91).
- **For the refit**: polling costs the GE nothing (`PollInstructions` as assumed); no term for work before the enqueue;
  the slowdown goes by the CPU's traffic beside the GE (round 10b's writer agrees with round 10's slowed writes); and a
  placement term for swizzled textures and palettes, by their base's offset (off 128 bytes 6 to 8% for texels, 5 to 6%
  for palettes; a multiple of 128 off 1 KiB 1.5 to 2%), which games' allocations decide.

### Not yet

- A burst of CPU work over part of a list (the spec's f): round 10b's writer outran every list, its clock looked at each
  turn; a burst shorter than the list (the clock looked at every 64 lines) would measure it.
- Placement of what else the GE and the CPU read: vertices, lists, and the two streams at chosen relative places (round
  10's re-runs moved RAM-to-RAM transfers 26% and the unswizzled `texture`'s cases 9 to 14% by where the arrays sat).
- The light registers' left-over kinds as a case of their own (a lone directional light shining after spotlights costs
  20.8 more a vertex).
